We have developed a comprehensive understanding of noncommutative quantum mechanics, especially in its phase space representation. In this context, the coordinates can be linked to differential operators that commute with each other, and they also correspond to specific classical Poisson brackets. When the momentum is not commuted, this leads to additional constraints that limit the possible forms of these operators. As a result, they can be explicitly represented as a set of harmonic oscillators in the noncommutative space. To enhance the distance margin of optical communication systems utilizing direct detection, a method is proposed that combines Weakly Nonlinear Equalization and Maximum Likelihood Sequence Estimation. By first applying WDFE to reduce burst errors, followed by MLSE to achieve near-ML performance, the system's sensitivity is increased. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through simulations, showing a significant reduction in burst errors and improved frame error rate performance when compared to a single-estimation approach. WDFE's ability to alleviate burst errors is found to enable MLSE to overcome more than 1 dB of margin, resulting in a 6 dB improvement in distance margin without MLSE's training overhead. The proposed method's performance is also found to approach the ideal ML performance after a certain increased margin is achieved. The speed penalty associated with MLSE is offset by the ability to use a shorter WDFE filter, allowing for a speed-up of the overall system by 50% while achieving near-ML performance. The proposed method's ability to compensate for burst errors and enable MLSE to approach ideal ML performance represents a significant breakthrough in the development of high-speed optical communication systems utilizing direct detection technology. Our innovative approach overcomes the current limitation of TCN models being model-size-sensitive, without requiring a trade-off with accuracy. Unlike conventional dilation methods that rely on ad-hoc techniques, our method achieves a significant improvement in performance while maintaining the TCN framework's simplicity. Our optimized model performed better than various state-of-the-art models, including Inception-TCN and Temporal Convolutional Network, in terms of efficiency. Additionally, our method can be applied to any TCN layer within a larger model. Our research demonstrates the potential of evolutionary computation to enhance the efficiency of complex neural network architectures. To analyze the performance of approximate message passing algorithms, particularly in the $	ext{Z}_2$-synchronization problem, researchers often examine the replica or TAP free energy as a benchmark. However, it has been observed that the TAP free energy may not accurately represent the behavior of these algorithms when the input symmetry does not match the model's symmetry. In such cases, the TAP free energy may appear optimal, yet the approximate message passing algorithm may still converge to suboptimal solutions. This study challenges the conventional notion that the TAP free energy always serves as a threshold for the convergence of approximate message passing algorithms. Instead, it shows that the TAP free energy may be achieved by the algorithm even when the underlying symmetry differs. As a result, the TAP free energy no longer acts as a reliable benchmark for evaluating the algorithm's performance. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the Bethe free energy, obtained through variational approximation, can provide a more accurate representation of the algorithm's behavior. This connection between the Bethe free energy and the algorithm's performance is established for the $	ext{Z}_2$-synchronization problem and generalizes previous results. In particular, it is shown that the algorithm's convergence and non-convergence are respectively characterized by the satisfiability of the loop-free and loop-satisfiability conditions in the corresponding factor graph. This relationship between the Bethe free energy and the algorithm's performance is then used to determine the storage capacity of the $	ext{Z}_2$-synchronization problem. It is found that the algorithm converges to the optimal solution when the underlying symmetry matches and converges to a suboptimal solution when the symmetries differ, with a threshold of approximately $2^{\theta(n)}$ based on a specific symmetry. Additionally, it is found that when the input symmetry is much stronger than the model's symmetry, the algorithm may still converge to a suboptimal solution with a threshold of approximately $2^{\sqrt{n}}$. This result provides a precise answer to a long-standing open question posed by Richard Urban and Amin Cooley. This study generalizes previous results on the $	ext{Z}_2$-synchronization problem to any symmetry and provides a general framework for analyzing the performance of approximate message passing algorithms based on the Bethe free energy. This framework can be applied to any discrete message passing algorithm and model with symmetry. Conversely, the runge-kutta algorithm with a fixed time step produced the lowest inaccuracy, but it also took the shortest time.  Interestingly, the gear method with a variable time step allowed for a significantly larger time step (0.0015 picoseconds) without a noticeable decrease in accuracy compared to the runge-kutta algorithm with a fixed time step (0.0003 picoseconds). We take a stable rational curve $C$ in $\mathbb{P}^1 \times \mathbb{P}^1$ with a symplectic volume of $4$ and investigate how its tropicalization and secondary polytope relate to the rational bitangents of a corresponding quartic surface $S$ in $\mathbb{P}^3$. These studies help us verify the conjectures of M\'ayorans-Dur\'an and Teitler, and further, we find the connection between the twisting of edges in the tropicalization and the rationality of these bitangents. Additionally, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between the edge twists and the rational bitangents, and this correspondence allows us to determine the number of rational bitangents through the coefficients of the tropicalization. For curves with a specific symmetry, we can even identify the rational bitangents by analyzing the faces of the secondary polytope. Lastly, we present an example to demonstrate that the number of rational bitangents can be any positive integer.

Conversational interfaces like voice assistants and virtual customer support systems deliver user value through automated conversations but also introduce a hard-to-detect issue: broken automation. When these systems malfunction, humans are typically redirected to handle the issue, wasting their time on problems already identified by the system's developers. To fix the problem quickly, the code causing it needs to be located immediately. Although automated testing frameworks are available, they often fail to detect existing bugs or take a long time to do so. Moreover, testing conversational systems is particularly difficult due to the random and slow nature of user interactions. This paper suggests a novel approach that uses the system's known flaws to create test cases, guaranteeing the detection of existing bugs. It also includes an efficient method to minimize the time required to run these test cases, making it suitable for the fast-paced development cycle of conversational system projects. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, it was applied to a voice assistant system, resulting in a significant reduction in testing time and a higher chance of detecting existing bugs. This approach was further shown to outperform traditional testing methods by detecting more bugs in the same amount of time. Additionally, it was compared to a method that uses machine learning to guess which parts of the code might be causing the problem, but the straightforward approach based on existing knowledge performed better. This approach can be applied to any stateless conversational system and encourages the development of more collaborative human and machine system testers. It is available online for the LLaMA-based Dialog system, which can be accessed at https://github.com/microsoft/dialog-testing. This approach led to a 2x faster detection of existing bugs in the LLaMA-based Dialog system and a 4x decrease in the chance of missing existing bugs. Prior studies have demonstrated that utilizing parallel corpora enhances neural machine translation (NMT) performance. By leveraging large scales of monolingual data and learning a bilingual seed model, cross-lingual memory retriever (CLR) enables NMT to access translated information even when no parallel data is available for the target language. This method allows translations to benefit from previously untranslated content in the target language, effectively expanding the available parallel data. Our research takes this concept a step further by utilizing monolingual datasets for both source and target languages in the CLR framework. This approach incorporates a bidirectional bilingual seed model that facilitates two-way language understanding. Models trained with CLR using monolingual data outperform traditional bilingual translation memory approaches and show significant performance gains, particularly when there is limited parallel data available. Our results indicate that CLR models perform well across low- to medium-resource settings and also translate longer sentences more effectively. Furthermore, we observe that CLR models exhibit lower monolingual data recall and most of the recalled data is translated accurately. This suggests that CLR effectively selects meaningful translations from monolingual datasets rather than random selections. Lastly, we find that CLR models handle style and domain adaptation more successfully than traditional methods. As the amount of monolingual data increases, the performance gap between CLR and traditional methods continues to expand. Additionally, while the bidirectional bilingual seed model plays a crucial role in CLR, it is not necessary to build this model on the largest available monolingual dataset. Instead, training on a more diverse dataset of monolingual data proves more effective. This approach prevents overfitting to a single dataset and enhances the ability to translate texts with different styles. In our experiments, we demonstrate that CLR outperforms traditional NMT models when evaluating test sets with styles or domains that are not present in the training data. This leads to significant improvements in domain adaptation settings and notable gains in style adaptation scenarios. As a byproduct of studying CLR in low-resource settings, we also obtain improved results on several medium-resource settings. To facilitate future research, we have made our models and data available for comparison and download. This includes the code, models, and datasets used in our experiments. In the domain of few-shot learning, various frameworks have been proposed that focus on constructing memory banks of average samples or employing distance metrics. Contraryely, the problem of outlier samples is often overlooked, which can significantly impede the convergence of optimization processes and ultimately the performance of models. To address this, we present a novel framework called TPS-Convolutional Graph Network (TPS-CGN), which effectively mitigates the influence of outlier samples through the use of transformation protocols and graph-structured models. Specifically, our model utilizes the thin-plate spline protocol to generate boundary protocols that can distinguish between in-distribution and out-of-distribution data, which are then applied to a convolutional graph network to refine prototypes. By representing prototypes as nodes in a graph structure and calculating inter-prototype distances, we effectively identify and downweight outlier samples. As a result, our model is able to effectively converge to optimal prototypes and achieve superior few-shot learning performance. Comprehensive experiments have validated the superiority of our approach, with performance improvements seen in episodic risk minimization, transfer learning, and data augmentation techniques. Our model also achieves remarkable flexibility in prototype selection and exhibits robust performance in the presence of hard outlier samples. With these capabilities, our model is well-suited for applications requiring robust convergence in the presence of outlier data. Code is available at: https://github.com/ghulghule/tps-cgn.

To address this limitation, we propose a protocol to systematically assess the generalization of user preference learning. Furthermore, we introduce the Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module, an adaptable module that identifies and amplifies the preferred aspects identified during training to improve recommendation accuracy. The GAPE module is incorporated into an attention-based recommendation system, demonstrating significant generalization improvements on various public datasets. The GAPE module's flexibility also allows it to be applied to other deep recommendation systems, leading to enhanced generalization performance. Our findings validate the effectiveness of generalization assessment and the GAPE module in promoting the discovery of preferred aspects and enhancing user preference learning. The effectiveness of medical AI models is heavily reliant on their training data.
If this data is biased, the model will likely produce similar results. For instance,
a model trained on diverse MRI scans using data from various sources may not
achieve the desired level of accuracy when tested on scans that were not part
of the training set. This phenomenon, where the model generalizes poorly to new
data, is often linked to data composition. However, the connection between data
composition and the model's performance can be complex and multi-faceted. To gain
a deeper understanding, we studied the impact of different data combinations
on the performance of MRI analysis models. Our findings revealed instances where
the model performed well on new data, despite data being somewhat diverse,
along with instances of poor performance on new data due to diverse data.
Additionally, we explored the connection between data composition and the
model's performance through various statistical measures. To improve the model's
performance on new data, we also tested different data selection methods.
These methods allowed us to choose the most effective data for training,
based on the model's performance. We applied these methods to three distinct
MRI analysis tasks and observed significant enhancements in the model's performance.
We achieved an average increase of 6.3% in the model's performance on new data,
as per the Dice similarity coefficient metric. We also discovered that the
best approach depends on both the data composition and the model architecture.
To facilitate replication and advancement of our findings, we have made our code
and data preparation protocol publicly available. Our study highlights the model's
sensitivity to data composition and encourages the development of fairer MRI
analysis models that can effectively utilize diverse data. These models should
be able to accurately interpret various types of MRI scans and minimize the
negative impact of data diversity on their performance. Consequently, they will be

The Motivation Dynamics (MD) model has been successfully applied to analyze various complex behaviors, including cooperation and competition among multiple agents. To further advance its practical applications, we develop a multi-agent MD model that incorporates relative distances, opaqueness, and asymmetry in its equations. This new model reveals a range of fascinating rendezvous behaviors and can be solved numerically to better understand the dynamics of clustering and dispersal phenomena. By comparing our model with the recently published work of Kolomiets and Ryhamat, we establish its theoretical validity and also demonstrate the MD model's ability to exhibit biologically plausible behavior in both numerical and graphical forms. Additionally, we explore possible connections between the model and real-world scenarios such as animal social interactions and provide possible directions for future research. As a result, the extended MD model presents new opportunities for studying complex interactions among multiple agents and can serve as a basis for analyzing cluster formation and coexistence in both mathematical and scientific contexts. Finally, we outline potential research paths to further validate the model and explore its applications in a broader context.

We investigated the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ system to study the effects of 5d/4f substitution on magnetic properties. Gd and Cm have distinct magnetic characteristics - Gd is an isolated magnetic moment with a spin of 7/2, while Cm exhibits multiple possible magnetic states and may show strong magnetic interactions. Our measurements reveal that the Gd-like moment remains relatively unchanged as the Cm composition increases, whereas the Ce-like moment enhances its magnetic contribution. Additionally, we observed a significant enhancement in the magnetic moment in the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ compounds, which may indicate a tendency towards magnetic ordering and long-range interactions within the 5d/4f system. Notably, the enhanced magnetic moment is directly correlated with the enhancement of the Kondo-like singlet-sensitivity and the breakdown of the heavy-fermion behavior in this system. We also analyzed the transport properties and found that the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ compounds exhibit non-Fermi liquid behavior, which is likely induced by the Cm composition and the disorder it causes. Our study offers a comprehensive understanding of the magnetic and transport properties within the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ system and sheds light on the complex interactions between 5d and 4f electrons in these compounds.

The structure of galactic halos remains an unsolved puzzle in astronomy. Furthermore, we derive the relationship between the observer's proper time and the invariant length, and establish the connection between the observer's four-velocity and the gradient of the potential function, which facilitates the identification of the mass-energy density within the spacetime. As a result, we are able to determine the expression for mass-energy density within the spacetime as a function of the observer's velocity and position. Finally, we illustrate that within the Fock approach, the gravitational field can be viewed as a manifestation of time-dependent mass-energy density, and that the gravitational field's source is linked to the structure of the spacetime itself. We re-examine the system of invariants established by Kirillov and Shubin that classify conjugacy classes in the symplectic group Sp(n,K). The original system used a combination of eigenvalues from the adjoint action and a Schur multiplier, as well as additional variables derived from moment maps and their Weyl group symmetries. However, our investigation reveals that these moment map variables can be eliminated, replaced by just the eigenvalues. This simpler form provides a direct correlation between the dynamics on Lie groups and their path group counterparts, potentially making it easier to study the latter. For instance, our results could facilitate a more accessible derivation of the centralizer in the symplectic group, which in turn might simplify the identification of irreducible representations in the symplectic Lie algebra. Our findings also reveal a striking analogy with the classification of conjugacy classes in the orthogonal group, which could have further implications for dynamics on Lie groups and their path group counterparts. Although our results are currently applicable to noncompact groups and thus may be amenable to analytical interpretations, future research is needed to explore connections with number theory.  Our results also raise the possibility that similar systems of invariants could be developed for other semisimple Lie groups, such as the general linear and special linear groups.

By combining the recommended items' topology from interaction graphs and their descriptive content using graph neural networks, entity representations can be both topologically and semantically informed, leading to improved performance in recommender systems. This novel approach to entity representation learning is what we call Topology-aware Entity Representation Learning. When these models are applied to broader domains like general knowledge, this tendency to group antonyms as synonyms becomes a significant hindrance. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach to building general-purpose embeddings that allows capturing the opposing meanings of words. This is achieved by introducing a new type of negative pairing for antonyms, which can be learned along with the usual positive similarities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by building financial sector embeddings and multi-domain embeddings and testing them on various tasks like identifying the antonyms of specific words and classifying the polarity of sentences. Our results show a notable improvement over the current state-of-the-art models. This approach also yields insights into the structure of financial concepts and the language used to describe the stock market. Moreover, we observe a notable improvement in the accuracy of sentiment classification, which is crucial for any financial text processing task. We have made our models and data available for further research and financial text processing applications. This paper explores the optimization of fair-throughput and sum-throughput in wideband waveforming techniques, considering a network with multiple co-existing systems. We demonstrate the potential for a hybrid approach that combines distributed and centralized waveforming, and analyze the resulting performance in terms of fair-throughput and sum-throughput. Next, we investigate the convergence of different waveforming methods, including DFT-based, DFT-precoded, and maximum-entropy based approaches, and examine how they cope with frequency-selective channels. Finally, a set of theorems is proposed to guide the selection of waveforming strategies based on the characteristics of the channel and system at hand. Through numerical simulations, we validate the efficacy of these theorems in ensuring optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput. Moreover, we showcase an implementation of the proposed theorems on a 5G testbed. Overall, this study provides a theoretical and practical framework for optimizing the performance of wideband waveforming techniques. Additionally, it paves the way for further research in this area, and highlights key considerations for the development of next-generation waveforming technologies.

In complex cooperative settings, player agents can quickly learn to bypass unappealing actions that lead to poor outcomes. We propose an innovative algorithm called comparative advantage regression learning (CAREL) that enables multiple learning agents to simultaneously discover and shun these actions. Unlike existing methods, CAREL uses a comparative advantage-based approach to compare each agent's action values and learn a distinguishing feature to identify and avoid the undesirable actions. We demonstrate that when one of the agents is an exploitative expert, learning jointly can lead to the discovery of the unwanted action. Furthermore, compared to other joint learning methods, our results show that CAREL accelerates this discovery. We also illustrate that when all agents are equal, learning jointly induces the discovery of all unwanted actions with certainty, which can be modulated through the variance of the feature learning process. Additionally, we highlight the advantages of CAREL in collaborative multiagent settings, including accelerating the discovery of action values and inducing the discovery of all action differences. To validate our approach in a realistic scenario, we present a data simulation where agents learn from reward information that is distorted by noise. Our results indicate that CAREL accelerates the discovery of action differences under noisy data. Our approach involves learning the systems' ability to understand the connection between actions and mental states through reinforcement learning. We demonstrated this approach's effectiveness with a sample task, and our results suggest that it can lead to more accurate human mental state inference. To facilitate further research, we have made our code and data available for public access. By building upon these findings and engaging in more dialog generation tasks, we can continue to advance the capabilities of these systems in understanding the thoughts and intentions of others. By categorizing concurrency conflicts as local or global, our framework provides a set of rules and guidelines to design conflict-resolution strategies, effectively reducing the difficulty of developing new CRDTs. Furthermore, our framework enables the generation of specific CRDT designs from abstract definitions, which can be utilized in popular programming languages. As a demonstration of our framework's efficacy, we created several renowned CRDTs, including replication, counter, multivalue counter, set, bag, rich counter, and multimapping counter, using Java as the implementation language. Our investigation reveals that FPN's ability to handle scale is its most notable advantage; however, objects of considerable size are frequently overlooked by the narrow bottom pyramid levels of these backbone networks. Understanding language involves navigating various complexities, including diverse contexts and multiple word forms within a single language. While machines have made significant progress in language processing, they often struggle with these challenges. This paper highlights the difficulties of building a machine that can accurately grasp language and proposes a novel approach, using a unique framework called Structured Differential Generalization. This framework combines the advantages of symbolic reasoning and neural networks to overcome the challenges. By testing the approach on two complex language understanding tasks - identifying referring expressions and interpreting navigation instructions - the results show that Structured Differential Generalization yields the most effective solution among various machine learning approaches. Furthermore, the method demonstrates a high degree of human-like performance and can also provide explicit proofs of its inferences. This approach facilitates a deeper understanding of how machines evaluate and make decisions about complex language. The code for this research is available on an open-source platform noted in the paper.

Most current computer vision work relies on ordered instructions and ignores the significant capabilities of humans who can follow unordered instructions to accomplish tasks. Despite significant progress in human-like performance on various tasks, machine learning models still struggle to sequence unordered instructions consisting of images, text, and other modalities, similar to how humans would. This study deviates from the usual path of ordering instructions and focuses on understanding unordered multimodal instructions. It assesses the machine learning models' ability to reason and sequence instructions of any order and tests their practical applications by using the instructions in real-world tasks. To achieve this, a large-scale dataset called "Unordered Instructions" was created containing 400,000 instructions of varying order for 50 different tasks. This dataset showcases machines' underperformance compared to humans and pushes the limit of machine learning models' capabilities to the same level of human-like performance on unordered instructions. This research also introduces novel evaluation metrics and cutting-edge machine learning models that can sequence unordered instructions. It demonstrates that machine learning models have a hard time compared to humans even when the instructions are semi-ordered. To address this challenge, the study proposes a new approach called the "Sequence-Augmented Model" that can effectively sequence unordered instructions with no extra cost when compared to traditional machine learning models. This model achieves state-of-the-art performance on various evaluation metrics in the newly created dataset and outperforms human-like performance for the first time. The study also explores the practical applications of machine learning models in following unordered instructions and demonstrates their capability to execute complex tasks with multiple steps using both real-world data and a household robot. This work represents significant progress in the field of computer vision that can understand unordered multimodal instructions and demonstrates machine learning models' capability to execute complex tasks with multiple steps similar to human capabilities. The impact of a large-scale event like an earthquake on a seismic network is significant and often underestimated. Although the focus typically lies on quick recovery measures, the long-term effect of these events is frequently disregarded. In this study, we investigate how the size of an earthquake affects the fragmentation of a network over an extended period by analyzing data from the Italian regional seismometer network between 2008 and 2015. We found that the network's connectivity declined significantly following large earthquakes within the specified time frame. Interestingly, the decrease in connectivity was not as pronounced when considering all earthquakes, but rather only those with a magnitude greater than 3.5. Furthermore, we observed a distinct fragmentation pattern in the network following a single node removal, which was influenced by the size of the resulting avalanche. Specifically, we found that increases in avalanche size led to greater network fragmentation. Additionally, we found that the maximum diameter of the affected area and the average distance between fault point locations were key factors in promoting post-earthquake fragmentation. In contrast, the earthquake's magnitude and magnitude of maximum deformation were less influential in this regard. Nonetheless, greater earthquakes generally led to greater fragmentation, although the relationship was not as direct. Rather, earthquakes with a magnitude of over 5.0 tended to cause greater network fragmentation. In conclusion, our research highlights the significance of examining the long-term effects of earthquakes on seismic networks and suggests that increased monitoring at key locations could be beneficial in mitigating post-earthquake fragmentation. Moreover, our study shows that even a single node removal can result in substantial network fragmentation, which can provide valuable insights for planning and implementing recovery strategies. Ultimately, our research paves the way for a more comprehensive understanding of the complex dynamics governing the fragmentation of seismic networks over an extended period. It also lays the groundwork for investigating additional factors that contribute to network fragmentation, such as non-seismic events, network evolution, and optimization of monitoring configurations. In doing so, our study will ultimately contribute to the development of more effective strategies for reducing the long-term effects of earthquakes on seismic networks. In the process, our research will also provide a deeper understanding of the underlying dynamics governing the fragmentation of these networks. In the long run, this will lead to the creation of more resilient and less prone-to-fragmentation networks that can adapt to changing conditions and withstand the impact of significant events. We propose a novel design for a gravitational wave detector, a sloshing-Sagncl interferometer, which incorporates a unique optical configuration and mirror suspension system. This design offers enhanced sensitivity by rectifying spatial stray light and minimizing phase noise. Additionally, our design can operate effectively even with imperfect mirrors, offering a promising solution to the challenge of designing reliable and efficient gravitational wave detectors. Through numerical analysis, we demonstrate the potential of the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer to surpass the sensitivity limitations of conventional detectors. However, our design also faces significant technical hurdles that must be overcome through innovative engineering solutions. Despite these challenges, the sloshing-Sagnac design represents an important step towards the development of highly sensitive and reliable gravitational wave detectors. Furthermore, its design may also be adapted for improved performance in other laser interferometer applications. 

This work is part of the PhD research conducted at the University of Oregon under the supervision of Peter Fritschel, a distinguished researcher in the field of gravitational wave science. Although the design itself holds significant value, the accompanying thesis provides a comprehensive exploration of the sloshing-Sagnac concept, delving into its theoretical foundations and incorporating a broader review of advanced gravitational wave detector designs.

By analyzing the performance of NOVR-XL RA in comparison to an ideal, non-cooperative baseline, we derive key insights into the system's behavior and identify critical factors that influence it. We also investigate the impact of different antenna array geometries and demonstrate the significant effectiveness of NOVR-XL RA through numerical simulations, showcasing substantial gains in random access performance. To further optimize NOVR-XL RA, we explore various multi-user scenarios and evaluate the system's performance under different user configurations. Notably, our results indicate that NOVR-XL RA can achieve near-optimal, system-sum rates in XL-MIMO systems. To facilitate practical implementation, we also propose a simplified protocol called NOVR-XL S and investigate its effectiveness. Through analysis and simulation, we demonstrate the efficacy of both NOVR-XL RA and NOVR-XL S. Finally, we discuss potential research paths for exploring other protocols and optimizing system design.

This study explores the potential impact of heavy neutral leptons on neutrino properties observed in high-energy particle collisions, specifically focusing on processes involving deep neural networks. Furthermore, the findings suggest that future experiments may be capable of identifying heavy neutral leptons with masses as low as 1 GeV. This could have important implications for the understanding of neutrino properties and their connection to the cosmological matter-antimatter asymmetry. We re-examine the operation of a Sagnac interferometer, particularly its behavior under conditions of high-speed motion, where relativistic effects become significant. By analyzing the consequences of the longitudinal Doppler shift on counter-propagating laser beams, we demonstrate that a relativistic Sagnac interferometer exhibits an imbalance in the phases of these beams, resulting in an additional phase difference that is directly proportional to the velocity of the observer. Notably, this additional phase difference is also present in the classical limit, albeit caused by a different mechanism related to time dilation and the relative motion of the interferometer's arms. Our findings provide a framework for understanding the phenomenon of frequency shift observed in relativistic Sagnac interferometry. Moreover, we derive a general expression that can be applied to multiple configurations of the interferometer, including those with internal sources and the Michelson-type design. Our predictions can be experimentally verified using high-speed and ultra-stable light sources, such as optical pulses from mode-locked lasers or continuous waves from atomic clocks. Finally, we outline the potential implications of achieving a detectable phase shift through high-speed optical pulses, such as observing quantum electrodynamics at very low energies or demonstrating the principle of quantum non-demolition measurement with relativistic precision.

In opposition to this conjecture, we present an instance where this conjecture holds true, albeit with the condition that the nilfibre in question cannot contain a dense path generated by a subgroup of operators in a certain high-dimensional space. This finding is significant because it allows us to prove a long-debated conjecture about the properties of Abelian varieties. The versatility of neural language models spans a wide range of applications, including machine translation, summarization, and text classification. To further boost their effectiveness, it is common to combine them with statistical $N$-gram models, a technique that involves sampling from the neural model and selecting the most probable outcome based on the $N$-gram model. Although this hybrid approach has been successful, using the neural model's output to inform the $N$-gram model and vice versa can lead to even better results. In fact, simply sharing the hidden states of the neural model with the $N$-gram model allows it to perform significantly better, indicating a sort of "neural transference" where the models learn each other's strengths. To take this a step further, we propose replacing the traditional sampling approach with a method that involves estimating the conditional distribution of the next word given the current context, both from the neural model and the $N$-gram model. We then develop an iterative process where the models make mutual predictions, resulting in the best possible outcome according to both models. We apply this hybrid approach to the tasks of machine translation, summarization, and language modeling itself, achieving substantial gains in performance, with improvements of up to 25%. Notably, our method yields the greatest benefits in scenarios with limited training data. We also discovered that this technique allows the use of smaller neural models, which results in additional efficiency gains. In the case of machine translation, we were able to reduce the size of the model by half without sacrificing performance when combining it with the $N$-gram model. We believe our findings have the potential to open up new avenues for the development of neural language models and their combination with statistical models. Our code is available at https://github.com/hahnfrido/LangAug. Our results also suggest that the hybrid approach may lead to a deeper understanding of how neural language models generate text, which we leave for future research to explore. Additionally, we observed that the hybrid approach results in a broader vocabulary usage, which we discuss in more detail in our paper. Lastly, we propose that this technique can be applied to a variety of other text-generation tasks, such as data-to-text systems, where the input is structured data and the output is human-readable text. In these scenarios, the generation process typically involves multiple iterations of the system, during which new data becomes available, which we believe makes our technique particularly well-suited. Creating a realistic three-dimensional face image from arbitrary poses requires a comprehensive understanding of both pose-dependent and pose-independent variations. Previous works that decomposed faces into discrete components or used low-dimensional models to capture variations, lacked the ability to achieve high-resolution details and accurate reconstructions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce the Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet), a high-fidelity model capable of analyzing a given face image and generating a detailed three-dimensional face mesh from zero. By employing a dual-framework structure with two nested networks that exchange encoded codes, our model effectively decomposes face images into pose-dependent and independent factors and reconstructs them accordingly. Through extensive experiments, our method demonstrates its superiority by achieving remarkable results on both synthetic and real-world data, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Notably, our approach successfully creates high-resolution face images (1024^3) in under three seconds, surpassing the performance of existing methods that struggle to handle such high-resolution inputs. To further demonstrate its applicability, we utilize our model to build a real-time face animation system, allowing for the manipulation of animated face videos using real-world face movements. The model's training speed and performance make it an attractive alternative to other complex speech synthesis models. A critical component of Nuclear Power Plants (NPPs) is their Residual Heat Removal (RHR) system, ensuring safe operation post-shutdown. These sensors can be vulnerable to cyber attacks, which could lead to incorrect temperature and pressure readings, potentially jeopardizing the safe functioning of the system. In this study, the vulnerability of these sensors to cyber attacks was investigated, which could result in the RHR system being switched to a safe state, thereby disabling the cooling process. In this state, the reactor could overheat, which could lead to a serious safety breach. As the transition to a low-carbon economy unfolds, storage technologies are emerging as a key component in the flexibility layer of future energy systems. To effectively manage these systems, policymakers need a deep understanding of how risk-averse storage operators behave under different incentives and market structures. Unfortunately, the current lack of empirical data on storage participation in existing markets hinders meaningful policy-making. In response, our novel framework utilizes equilibrium analysis to model the decisions of risk-averse storage providers within a multi-unit market setup, where different generators and storage devices compete to supply power. We establish a clear testable hypothesis regarding the comparative statics of storage size in response to varying parameters, including the value of beta, a key indicator of risk aversion. To validate our theoretical model, we employ an existing approach to estimate parameters and obtain initial conditions. With these parameters in place, we utilize a stylized numerical example to explore how storage size reacts to changes, especially under different levels of risk aversion, and even in the absence of wind. Our results show that increased risk aversion leads to smaller storage sizes, with the exact storage response depending on the market structure and other factors like the marginal cost of traditional generators. Interestingly, when wind power is introduced, the storage size actually increases in some cases, helped by the opportunity to sell negative marginal value benefits. Notably, our findings also indicate that in some market scenarios, storage size may still vary when there is no wind, driven by the potential for arbitrage. Ultimately, our storage policy prescriptions, derived from equating the storage provider's marginal value to costs in different market states, offer relevant guidance for policymakers navigating this complex and rapidly evolving energy landscape. To facilitate replication and further exploration, we have made our Python code openly available. Our study offers a new perspective on the long-lasting dust storms on Mars, specifically the great southern storm that persisted for 250 Earth days in 2007. By analyzing data from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and the Mars Science Laboratory and using computer simulations of the Martian atmosphere, we discovered that the massive storm was part of a global circulation pattern driven by temperature differences. This circulation pattern shared similarities with baroclinic storms on Earth and atmospheric circulation patterns in a hypothetical Earth-like atmosphere. As the storm moved northward, it was halted by the mid-latitude mountain range on Mars, causing the persistent plume. The storm was eventually seen dissipating in images from the Mars Orbiter, suggesting that it may have been influenced by the CO2 polar dry ice caps, which could provide a source of dust and heat. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and understand the full extent of the Martian atmosphere's circulation patterns. These storms could also pose a risk to any potential human missions to the planet. 

By comparing the Martian storm to the 2004 European heat wave and the 2012 United States drought, which were caused by similar atmospheric patterns, we found that the Martian storm had a similar level of severity. However, the storm's impact on the Martian surface was minimized due to the planet's thin atmosphere, which allowed heat to escape freely. In contrast, the increased greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere are intensifying heat waves and droughts on our planet.

Current active learning methods often select a fixed number of data points for human labeling, which may not be effective for large datasets like ImageNet. This is because these datasets are composed of many categories, some with limited representation, making it crucial to prioritize categories with few examples. Existing approaches typically focus on individual data points, neglecting the structural organization of categories. To address this shortcoming, we propose an active learning framework called Category-Averaged Distance (CAD) that averages the distances of data points within each category to determine a category's uncertainty. This approach allows for dynamic selection of data points for labeling, taking into account the inherent diversity of large datasets like ImageNet. In evaluations using the ImageNet dataset, our method demonstrates superior performance compared to traditional active learning approaches. Additionally, our results show that CAD is more efficient than selectively sampling data points based on category uncertainty. To facilitate replication and advancement of active learning methods on large datasets like ImageNet, we release our code and dataset sampling strategy at https://github.com/whonyy/cad. Our evaluation protocol, which prioritizes data efficiency and category-based diversity, serves as a benchmark for future research to tackle large-scale active learning challenges.

Through a combination of analytical and numerical approaches, we gain a deeper understanding of how the algebraic multiplicity evolves during the Schur process. Our theoretical and computational results provide concrete bounds and illustrate the concept of our new definition with specific examples. Airports are vulnerable to theft and terrorism due to the lack of x-ray technology effectiveness in detecting hidden items. To address this issue, we introduce HiXray, the first dataset of its kind that uses x-ray images to identify concealed objects. HiXray consists of 8000 scans containing 100 categories of forbidden items, with a focus on hard-to-detect objects like liquids, biological substances, and explosives. To enhance the performance of models in concealed object detection, we developed a comparative analysis using state-of-the-art architecture incorporating encoder decoder and transformer patterns. Experimental results reveal our approach surpasses existing solutions and provides robust item detection across poses, with hidden items detected at a 0.78 Average Accuracy rate. To facilitate further progress in this research area, we have made the dataset and project code available on GitHub. With improved techniques and data, we believe x-ray technology now has the capability to effectively identify hidden items, reducing the risk of security breaches at airports. The concept of the Hankel path serves as a foundation for extending the Gamma function, as well as other specific functions like the Riemann zeta function, to the complex plane. By defining a contour integral using a Hankel path, we can express functions in a way that reveals their analytic properties. This paper specifically explores the extension of the Gamma function to the complex plane through the Hankel representation. It begins by establishing the relationship between the traditional Gamma function and its Hankel representation. Further, it identifies conditions under which the Hankel representation can be utilized to analyze the function's convergence and continuity. Subsequent sections investigate the relationship between the Hankel representation and other complex functions, including the zeta function, as well as its connections to the saddle point method and the Riemann-van der Monde identity. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a unified framework for extending functions to the complex plane using Hankel paths and contour integrals.

This paper provides novel proofs for several identities derived from the Hankel representation of the Gamma function. It also explores a connection to the zeta function, revealing a relationship that can be used to analyze the zeros of the zeta function. By leveraging this relationship, we can demonstrate the non-existence of zeros on specific contours in the complex plane. Additionally, this relationship enables us to examine the distribution of zeros along these contours. It is demonstrated that the zeros conform to a specific logarithmic growth pattern, mirroring the behavior of the Riemann Hypothesis for whole numbers. This framework for complex function analysis through Hankel paths may have broader applications, enabling the extension of other functions that can be represented through contour integrals. The development of privacy-preserving learning through differentially private methods like stochastic gradient descent is gaining momentum. However, existing analyses of privacy loss under data connectivity in graph structures are yet to be explored thoroughly. This work delves into the complexities of privacy loss computation in connected data points, specifically focusing on Euclidean space representations. It outlines novel algorithms for approximating private data points' connections and leverages these to compute lower bounds on privacy loss for low-dimensional data sets. Furthermore, we demonstrate the challenges and limitations of these methods in high-dimensional settings through experimental evaluations. The findings highlight significant difficulties in achieving reliable privacy guarantees in high-dimensional scenarios compared to lower-dimensional scenarios. The developed methods are further applicable to various learning tasks, including support vector machines. The results show that approximating private data points' connections becomes increasingly complicated as the dimensionality reduces, as evidenced by the rapid decline in error bounds in our empirical studies. The results also indicate that the error in approximating connections can drop by as much as 10,000 times when decreasing the dimensionality from 10,000 to 10 in certain configurations. The research into computational complexity and lower bounds provides valuable insights and can be adapted for analyzing the privacy loss in other learning algorithms. The challenging nature of high-dimensional data is highlighted by the significant difficulties that arise even with the simplest of methods, as demonstrated by the sharp decline of error bounds in our empirical studies, indicating that the error in approximating the connection can drop by as much as 10,000 times, as seen in certain configurations, when the dimensionality drops from 10,000 to 10. The study's findings can aid the development of more efficient differentially private learning algorithms, especially those tailored for high-dimensional data sets. The research also introduces a new approach, the ball union algorithm, which computes the privacy loss bound by approximating private data points as if they were connected by rolling balls of a specific size. The algorithm is then used to derive lower bounds on privacy loss for low-dimensional data sets. The study expands the application of these methods to various learning tasks, including support vector machines, and examines the challenges and limitations of the algorithms in high-dimensional settings through experimental evaluations, demonstrating the difficulties in achieving reliable privacy guarantees in high-dimensional scenarios compared to lower-dimensional scenarios. The study's novel algorithms for approximating private data points' connections can be used to compute lower bounds on privacy loss for low-dimensional data sets, offering a novel perspective on computational complexity and lower bounds. We present a novel linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme for evaluating quantum correlation functions, based on an equilibrium hydrodynamic description and modified by the inclusion of quantum forces. This new method overcomes the limitation of previous approaches to tackle nonequilibrium situations, as demonstrated in a calculation of time-dependent quantum correlation functions for a quantum gas in the vicinity of a phase transition. The linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme is compared to a traditional hydrodynamic method and shown to be more accurate in nonequilibrium situations, while requiring only half the computational cost for the same level of precision. The benefits of the linearized scheme are its efficiency and simplicity, making it an appropriate tool for the large-scale simulation of quantum systems undergoing rapid changes. The algorithm can be extended to include quantum fluctuations by employing the Lindblad approach. The performance of the linearized scheme is showcased with simulations of quantum phase transitions in a quantum gas confined by an oscillating harmonic trap and interacting electrons experiencing sudden changes in their mutual coupling. The results highlight the capability of the linearized scheme to accurately simulate quantum correlations in large systems undergoing rapid transformations. The algorithm is designed to be highly parallelizable and is suitable for large-scale simulations of quantum systems in nonequilibrium situations. The implementation of the algorithm in the SALMON extender for quantum hydrodynamics (SQH) enables the simulation of quantum systems comprising millions of particles. The simulation of quantum phase transitions in large systems or those experiencing sudden changes is one example of the kind of research that can be performed with this algorithm. The source code of the SALMON SQH is an open-source code available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/jpn-group/salmon-sqh. The results of the calculations discussed in this paper can be found in the supplementary material. Recent action proposal generation methods primarily focus on extracting visual features
from single images, ignoring the potential benefits of additional context. To address
this limitation, we introduce the Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN), which leverages
context from both individual elements and combined features within boundaries defined
by pre-generated proposal boxes. By doing so, our network is able to extract local
features and aggregate global context, simultaneously. To facilitate context access
and weight optimization, we employ linear transformations at multiple context levels.
Contexts are then combined using additive and modulated concatenation, followed by
spatial score aggregation. Experimental results demonstrate that DCAN achieves superior
performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, including enhanced average
precision and reduced inference time. Moreover, DCAN proves computationally more
efficient in terms of parameter reduction. To facilitate replicable research, the
DCAN code and proposals will be hosted on the MMAction2 repository.

It is also argued that better understanding of the magnetic island interaction and its impact on the edge of a tokamak will be crucial for developing more accurate models of ELM onset. To create a more realistic and effective robot collision avoidance system, we suggest modifying a previous approach by incorporating the concept of a repulsive potential field into the robots' velocity commands. By adding a virtual force that counters the gradient of a potential field, we can prevent the robots from entering areas with increasing negative potential. To enhance the performance of this method in managing concurrent robot interactions, we explore alternative definitions of the potential field. After analyzing various configurations, we find that incorporating vorticity into the potential field's definition yields superior results. To facilitate simultaneous robot interactions, we establish a boundary condition that effectively reduces the number of influencing robots. To verify the efficacy of our proposed method, we conduct a series of experiments utilizing a simulation tool. Results indicate that the proposed approach outperforms the original system in handling concurrent robot interactions, and that the optimal potential field definition helps optimize performance. Moreover, we find that the method's best practice indeed emerges when considering the infinite number of influencing robots. To make the approach applicable to actual robot experiments, we explore ways to downscale the virtual force's effect on physical robots. Finally, we demonstrate the method's effectiveness in preventing collisions with a swarm of physical robots. Additionally, we investigate the impact of distinct velocity command controllers on the robots' movement patterns. To further the development of this approach, we suggest potential improvements and consider the implications for the movement of robots in a continuous, three-dimensional space. Lastly, we make the algorithm publicly accessible on an online repository.

Given a 2-fold covering map $p: X \to Y$ between connected, oriented closed surfaces of genus at least 2, we investigate the concept of relatively 1-homotopic maps from $X$ to the space of harmonic maps from $X$ to itself, with target being the 2-sphere. By utilizing an infinite sequence of operators defined through the Mayer-Vietoris sequence for harmonic maps, we establish the vanishing of specific homotopy groups. Consequently, this leads to a key conclusion about the triviality of certain homotopy groups, which in turn enables us to classify these relatively 1-homotopic maps. Ultimately, our classification results yield new proofs for certain previously established facts about the solvability of certain Plateau problems. Moreover, our approach also gives rise to new questions related to the symplectic Plateau problem. Lastly, our method of determining harmonic map orbits also paves the way for exploring similar issues in other contexts.

We investigate the long-term behavior of solutions to a particular nonlinear parabolic equation. By analyzing the properties of a associated Hamiltonian, we find that its stability or instability determines the asymptotic outcome. Specifically, if the equilibrium point is stable, solutions that initially diverge from it will converge back to it over time. Conversely, if the equilibrium point is unstable, solutions will continue to diverge from it. This outcome applies regardless of their initial values. If the Hamiltonian has neutral stability at the equilibrium point, solutions may either converge to another solution or exhibit oscillatory behavior around the equilibrium point. This study is relevant to a broad class of Ginzburg-Landau type equations and their equivalents. It provides a more refined understanding of the equation's solutions and their long-term behavior. It also enables the identification of critical values in parameters that mark significant changes in solutions' dynamics. It achieves this by establishing a hierarchy of relative stability for the equilibrium point and its solutions. This hierarchy is determined by the Hamiltonian's stability at the equilibrium point. By changing the packing density, we distinguish between jamming points in stress states and find different exponents characterizing the spectra of these points.  We find that the frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming have the same critical exponent but different exponents for frictionless shear jamming and isotropic frictional jamming.  We also find that the frictionless shear jamming has a unique exponent compared with other stress states. We further find that the diversity of stress states is linked with the diversity of force networks through the distribution of constraints and the spatial intermixing of force directions, and we propose that such an understanding can be applied to general central force networks. The process of identifying optimal protocol configurations from numerous possibilities is a challenging problem that can be solved using a technique called configuration exploration. However, this approach is often impractically slow, causing the community to adopt limited, yet ineffective configurations to ensure timely results. We introduce BoAnon, an innovative search algorithm that efficiently discovers high-quality configurations by learning from previously tested, low-quality ones. BoAnon uses a balance of diverse sampling strategies to evaluate different configurations, leveraging their shared characteristics to refine its assessment. By combining these strategies, BoAnon significantly outperforms traditional methods and other configuration exploration approaches. Additionally, BoAnon's ability to adapt to new protocols is remarkably swift, taking only a small fraction of the time required for the protocol to be fully understood. We demonstrate BoAnon's capabilities by using it to develop an efficient configuration for the BAWL protocol, achieving a substantial improvement of 50% or more in performance compared to other methods. Furthermore, BoAnon's performance is diverse, varying from a 25% improvement to a 75% reduction in transactions and message exchanges, and BoAnon's results are applicable to other protocols as well. We have made BoAnon available for other researchers to use and employ in their own work. By making this tool publicly available, we hope to encourage collaboration and contribute to the development of more efficient blockchain protocols. This study examines the transverse momentum dependence of triangular flow $v_3$ and elliptic flow $v_2$ for pions, kaons, and protons within the 30-40% centrality range of Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV. Measured up to a pseudorapidity of 0.8, the coefficients of $k_T$-weighted $v_n$ are compared across different particles, revealing an inverse trend between $v_2/k_T$ and $v_3/k_T$. Additionally, particle species' $v_3/k_T$ exhibits a similar $k_T$ dependence as $v_2/k_T$, albeit with a greater magnitude. Furthermore, this similarity is observed across various transverse momenta and centrality intervals, and is further explored in relation to system size and temperature through relativistic heavy ion collision simulations. The findings are also interpreted in terms of initial condition geometry and its impact on particle flow phenomena. Lastly, this study highlights the significance of $v_3$ measurements in understanding the underlying mechanisms driving flow phenomena, and advises for future studies involving identified particles in heavier system sizes.

We examine a Cayley tree with a finite connection number and an Ising model that exhibits duality. By applying the methods of group representation, we find that the self-duality condition results in the rotation group being reduced to a cyclic permutation within the space of spins that are mutually equivalent. Additionally, we determine the critical temperature by using an explicit transfer matrix, and conclude that the structure of the Ising model on a Cayley tree with self-duality and finite connection number is equivalent to a Diophantine equation that has a root that is an irrational golden ratio. Furthermore, we derive an exact expression for the logarithmic singularity of the system's free energy at the critical temperature, and predict that the system exhibits a non-trivial phase transition with power-law behavior. Our results generalize those found in [Phys. Rev. E 97, 032104 (2018)] for star-like connected graphs. Moreover, our findings provide a foundation for further study and generalization to more complex graph structures. Lastly, we outline the implications of our work for the solubility of the step-wise free energy equation that arises from the Lagrange multipler method.

This paper introduces a novel iterative method, called the Preconditioned Nonstandard FGMRES (PNFGMRES) for addressing numerical challenges. The standard FGMRES iteration is widely adopted for linear systems, especially when dealing with sparse systems that have limited connectivity. However, it can sometimes lead to ill-conditioned matrices in its residual basis. To mitigate this issue, the PNFGMRES approach modifies the iteration by incorporating an additional term derived from the maximum principle, which enforces non-negativity and bounds the absolute values of the approximate solutions. To demonstrate the effectiveness of PNFGMRES, several test cases are considered, including a simple diffusion problem, a Keller-Segel system, a Mersen-Poincar\'e problem, and the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, all of which exhibit slow convergence or failed convergence with the standard FGMRES. In contrast, the PNFGMRES method successfully yields convergent and accurate numerical solutions for these systems. The implementation of the PNFGMRES algorithm also involves a parametric relaxation technique to balance the additional term, which allows for flexible weight parameters to be adjusted according to the specific requirements and challenges of each system. To further enhance the convergence rate, the PNFGMRES method can be combined with a outer iteration technique, where the outer iteration iterates over different weights. Notably, all the simulated test cases converge to the desired equilibrium state, which is indicative of the method's ability to effectively manage the absolute bound of the solutions. To evaluate the PNFGMRES method, the convergence rate and computational time are examined across various systems and challenge levels. The results show that the PNFGMRES method achieves a comparable or superior convergence rate to the standard FGMRES method, while the computational time exhibits a broader range of variation. To further explore the nonstandard FGMRES method, the paper also examines the effect of the relaxation parameter in the inner iteration, which demonstrates that the optimal convergence rate can be achieved with a relatively small number of inner iterations. To extend the applicability of the PNFGMRES method, the paper also considers non-Newtonian preconditioning, which involves replacing the Hessian matrix with a non-Newtonian multigrid method. The results indicate that the non-Newtonian preconditioning can significantly improve the convergence rate of the PNFGMRES method, which further highlights the method's potential for addressing a broader range of challenging systems. The PNFGMRES method is implemented using the PETSc library and the FGMRES solver

The concept of conformal matter collineations is examined in this research for degenerate and semi-degenerate energy-momentum tensors.  For the latter, previously established results regarding conformal collineations are built upon, leading to an expanded understanding that applies to both tensor types.  A specific example, involving the Einstein field equations, is analyzed to demonstrate the applicability of these concepts.  Our investigation yields the number of degrees of freedom for conformal collineations in both degenerate and semi-degenerate scenarios.  Additionally, this research explores the relationship between conformal collineations and the symmetries of the energy-momentum tensor. While self-supervised flow estimation has achieved notable progress, several complications remain fully resolved, particularly in regards to occlusions. Our study posits that incorporating occlusions as a normal aspect of scene dynamics enables the learning of robust feature descriptors. To facilitate this learning, we developed a method to automatically identify and mask occlusive areas within images. By integrating occlusion detection with a masking process, we created a self-supervised approach for estimating flow that incorporates an occlusion mask. However, incorporating this mask also introduces an issue of mask propagation through the estimation process. To address this challenge, we introduced a modified occlusion mask propagation technique that considers both occlusive areas and scene parallax. Our approach, when tested against established self-supervised and supervised methods on the MPI-SMT and ADE20K datasets, showed superior performance according to metric scores. Additionally, our method's robust feature learning capabilities were validated through ablation tests on the Librisoft dataset. Our approach also offers a novel perspective on mask propagation, enabling future research in the topic. All code and datasets employed in this study are available for access at https://github.com/linguozh/ocflow.

However, there is a lack of studies focusing on the average performance of these models against diverse datasets. This paper proposes a new, general-purpose classifier, with 11 fully connected neurons, that can compete with the accuracy of traditional artificial neural networks in a low-power consumption model, suitable for mobile devices. We also observed a notable correlation between the model's performance and dataset size. As the number of samples increases beyond 500, the model's performance also tends to improve. A 3-allied set in a graph G is a collection of three vertices that are connected by edges, and for the purpose of this concept, the neighboring edges are considered as an X-shaped configuration. Even-2-factorable (E2F) refers to the ability of assigning even degrees to the rungs of a 3-allied framework within a graph. This property can also be viewed as identifying even-length paths that connect pairs of adjacent vertices while passing through other adjacent vertices. Our research focuses on determining the equivalent conditions and properties of E2F in the context of general cubic graphs, and we explore the connection between even-2-factorable graphs and those with 1-factors that consist of even-length paths. Additionally, we establish the relationship between even-2-factorable graphs and certain subgroups of the automorphism group of a cubic graph. This leads to a more general conclusion that the intersection of two even-2-factorable cubic graphs contains a 2-factorable subset. We apply our findings to specific types of cubic graphs, including those from the family of Cayley graphs generated by the alternating group A_n, and we present a novel approach to determining the E2F property in these graphs based on the parity of the number of elements in the generating set. Our results also provide a general framework for identifying even-2-factorable graphs within the family of cubic association schemes, and this is demonstrated through the determination of an E2F condition for a specific type of cubic graph characterized by its dual. Our research also delves into the exploration of even-2-factorable graphs and their connection to circulant graphs, as well as considering the implications for E2F property in the context of graph degeneracy. Our study also leads to the identification of a new class of E2F graphs, referred to as double-group graphs, and their associated properties. Our results conclude with the determination of E2F property in various double-group graphs, and this is achieved through the application of our general framework for E2F graphs based on the structure of their group generators. Our research expands the current understanding of even-2-factorable graphs and their properties, and this paves the way for further exploration and generalization in the context of higher allied degrees. Timeloops is a cutting-edge technique that enables system call filtering for various applications, even those written in interpreted languages such as PHP, Python, and Ruby. Unlike conventional system call management, which relies on loading modified application code, Timeloops allows for system call redirection through a specialized kernel module. This kernel module maps a original system call function to a replacement function, which the application can then use to execute different actions. By doing this, a significant boost in performance can be achieved, and it also becomes much harder for cyber attackers to exploit system call-based vulnerabilities. Our research takes this approach a step further by adapting Timeloops to work with virtual machines used in cloud computing, specifically KVM. We also demonstrate the feasibility of this approach with Python-based applications. Our findings indicate that while there is some performance loss compared to the original system, the boosted security could potentially make up for this loss. Additionally, we discovered that the biggest performance hindrance is not the underlying technology but rather the Python interpreter itself. Nonetheless, we believe that our research has the potential to inspire further innovation and exploration in the field of cloud security. Our source code is available for download at https://github.com/CS4243-Timeloops.

Our derivation of the exact decay rate of initial conditions in a controlled system is based on an interior observability result for a related simplified system, achieved by approximating the original system with a system possessing stronger dissipative properties. The proposed approach facilitates the use of observability inequalities in modeling population extinction, addressing concerns about validity of classical uniform bounds for certain nonlinear systems. The primary technical contribution of this study involves the development of an innovative strategy to overcome difficulties posed by nonhomogeneous coefficients and nonlinear interactions, leveraging the concept of partial regularization. The resulting decay rate estimate is remarkably concise and universally applicable. The way players, coaches, and fans perceive actions in soccer is not the same as their actual impact on the game. To provide a more accurate understanding, we can compare the potential consequences of actions like committing a foul, causing the ball to go out, or going for a shot. By using counterfactuals to what actually happened, we can determine how likely each action was. Using data from the 2020 UEFA European Football Championship, we found that players are about 2.5 times more likely to shoot the ball when it goes out of bounds, and about 1.5 times more likely to commit a foul when a free kick is awarded to the opposing team. Additionally, we found that players are more likely to commit a foul when a goal kick is taken (about 1.3 times more likely) and when a direct free kick is awarded (about 1.2 times more likely). We also found that players are more likely to shoot the ball when it goes out of bounds in about 27% of cases, and when the ball is given to the opposing team for an indirect free kick in about 21% of cases. We used a Bayesian approach to account for the limited number of observations in some situations. We believe our method can be applied to any action that occurs in a finite number of instances, such as offside positions or direct free kicks. We also think our research can contribute to a deeper understanding of soccer gameplay. We observed that players shoot the ball when it goes out of bounds, which could indicate a lack of communication among players or ineffective decision-making. We also found evidence suggesting that players do not fully understand the indirect free kick situation, which could indicate a need for adjustments to the game's rules. We propose that the sport's governing body provide players with clear guidelines on what constitutes an indirect free kick, and consider introducing a 'kick-off' style free kick for situations like this. We believe our research can lead to a more accurate and engaging broadcast of the sport. This paper investigates the fundamentals of a combined data and energy transfer model in a 2-dimensional Discrete Memoryless Channel, utilizing the Time-Fixed Intermittent Energy Transfer scheme. We derive optimal strategies for encoding data and energy at the sender, as well as decoding at the receiver, and examine the system's performance when considering various energy costs. We also investigate special cases, including the scenario where the receiver has an unlimited capacity to store energy. We demonstrate that through efficient energy allocation, the TFIET scheme achieves the highest data transfer rate, compared to non-intermittent energy transfer methods. Furthermore, we find that when energy costs are negligible, the optimal strategy simplifies to first-in-first-out data transfer. This paper delves into the reasons why standard Recurrent Neural Network models fail to achieve comparable performance to state-of-the-art Dialogue Understanding tasks and offers a comprehensive analysis of their internal representations. By comparing RNN and Transformer models based on various performance metrics and representation evaluation methods, our findings reveal that Transformers exhibit distinct representation dynamics, capturing more relevant contextual information. To rectify RNN's performance shortfalls, we introduce a simple adaptation technique, leveraging a representation extraction method called Multivariate Linear Discriminant Analysis. This technique enhances RNN models by selecting the most contextually significant features from their hidden states, allowing them to demonstrate improved accuracy on several popular Dialogue Understanding tasks. Our method demonstrates notable success, with the adapted RNN models achieving performance on par with Transformer models. Code is available at: https://github.com/ChenChen312/DA-MLDA.

Through a series of tests, our approach demonstrates superior detection rates when compared to traditional methods and is robust in navigating through various and ever-changing environments.
