The use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for identifying and segmenting areas of interest in medical imaging has become increasingly prominent. As a complementary region, the Medula Cerebellar (Cerebellar Peduncles) has been overlooked in analysis and research. This paper introduces a novel approach that employs a cascading strategy, dividing the task into two separate CNNs: one for detecting and outlining the Cerebellar Peduncles, and another for refining the segmentation. This approach was successfully applied to automatically segment the Cerebellar Peduncles in MRI scans as part of the 2020 BigBrain BigData Challenge. Our results demonstrate competitive performance, achieving the third highest Dice coefficient (0.79) among all competition entries. The methodology presented in this paper offers a valuable reference for the study of Medula Cerebellar and may also be adapted for similar applications in other brain regions. We demonstrate that using unextendible product bases instead of separable states can achieve strong quantum nonlocality in multipartite systems. Furthermore, we show that applying this approach allows us to find quantum nonlocality more efficiently. As an example, we determine the strong quantum nonlocality present in four parties of twenty-four possible situations. Our findings also reveal instances of quantum nonlocality based on entanglement witnesses, outperforming previously known results which were limited to two-party scenarios. These findings provide valuable insights into the properties of quantum nonlocality within multipartite systems.

By dividing the sky into discrete pixels and assigning a score to each based on its scientific value, we leverage an evolutionary algorithm to find the most efficient and safest trajectory. To speed up computation, we implement a co-evolutionary approach that divides the search into multiple sub-problems. To prevent astrobots from colliding with existing trajectories, we develop a collision avoidance filter, and to minimize overlapping observations, we introduce an intra-trajectory optimization step. The Group Lasso method has been widely adopted for selecting important variables from continuous or categorical data, including those taking the form of graphs or matrices. This algorithm adds a penalty to the least squares function, discouraging some variables from being part of a model. Building on the Group Lasso idea, we developed the Mixed Lasso model, which allows variables to be grouped in diverse structures such as graphs, matrices, and categorical pairs. Our algorithm combines the Group Lasso penalty with an additional constraint that restricts sparsity within each group, resulting in a solution where some group members are selected while others are penalized. We established the consistency of our estimator and provided a step-by-step path to solve the problem using alternating directions, followed by a discussion on its applicability to various mixed-type datasets. Through simulated and real-world experiments, the performance of the Mixed Lasso was compared to other state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its superiority in variable selection. All of our code can be accessed through the Mixed Lasso package on the RForge platform. This preprint investigates the applications of Weyl group cosets in analyzing degenerate Eisenstein series, extending the findings of Bruberg, Mui, and Mui which dealt with non-degenerate cases. Bruberg, Mui, and Mui's work built upon the framework of Gelfand-Serganov and Shintani, which connected degenerate Eisenstein series with Galois covers of Shimura varieties. The study is set within the context of a specific reductive group $G$ defined over a number field $F$, along with a non-trivial Borel subgroup $B$ containing a maximal torus $T$. The group $W_0$, or the Weyl group generated by the reflections $s_\alpha$ for all $\alpha$ in the absolute Galois group $\hat{G}_F$, is used to analyze the degenerate Eisenstein series. The research also explores the relationship between these series and Galois covers of certain Shimura varieties, including Drinfeld's cover of the Rapoport-Zink space, enabling the computation of certain L-functions. The study further generalizes the results of Bruberg, Mui, and Mui to a broader family of groups $G$ that includes $GL_2$ and $GSp_4$. The research provides a computationally verifiable conjecture, enabling the calculation of the L-function $\Lambda_{S(\phi)}$ for a broad family of fundamental algebraic objects $\phi$. The study also introduces a new set of operators, dubbed Hecke-Laxton operators, which extract the central critical value from an L-function, and explores their properties. The research concludes with an open question regarding the field of definition for Galois covers of Shimura varieties. Following the 2016 data taking period, the CMS detector at the LHC underwent significant upgrades to enhance its sensor material and readout technology. The silicon pixel detector, a central component of the detector, was replaced with an improved version featuring an upgraded layout and enhanced readout architecture. This upgraded detector, comprising three distinct layers and 80 million pixels, featured enhanced hit identification capabilities and reduced readout thresholds. As a result, the detector's overall performance saw a notable enhancement. This paper delves into the detailed optimization processes and presents the outcomes of the beam qualification tests conducted in 2015, 2016, and 2017, highlighting the advancements achieved with the new detector design. The results show a significant reduction in hit efficiency at low energies and improved track reconstruction in dense environments. Additionally, the upgraded detector demonstrated the ability to accurately measure the curvature of high-momentum particles. These advancements resulted in the capability to precisely measure a range of key physics parameters, including the detection of lepton momentum up to 4 TeV, the measurement of heavy flavor jets, and the search for high-transverse-momentum Higgs bosons. This enhanced performance, coupled with the increased luminosity available through the LHC's upgrade to 3000 fb$^{-1}$ by 2023, will enable the discovery or the rejection of various new physics scenarios by a 5$\sigma$ level of confidence. This paper outlines the design, performance, and anticipated outcomes of the upgraded CMS pixel detector, which is currently being installed on the detector and is on track for full integration by the end of 2023. Once operational, this upgraded detector will play a pivotal role in the search for new physics phenomena in high-energy collisions. A review is provided of the glueball spectrum as it stands in 2003, with a focus on recent developments up to the end of 2002. The quantum chromodynamics field has been explored through various methods such as lattice computations, scalar meson sum rules, and charmonium dispersion relations to identify its underlying characteristics and potential connections to quantum field theory's renormalization group properties. The review updates previous estimates of the glueball mass spectrum and discusses the implications of the data collected. It is suggested that a fully functional Higgs operator could be found by investigating the lattice representation of the trace of the square of the gluon field, a concept previously mentioned in the context of magnetic monopoles and topological transitions. The review also presents a new approach to computing the glueball mass spectrum directly from the quantum chromodynamics Lagrangian. The discussion concludes with an analysis of how the lattice representation of quantum chromodynamics might be connected to the bosonic string theory known as Hilbert-Sato strings. The review highlights the need for a more dynamic approach to computing quantum chromodynamics' observables and suggests the utility of characterizing glueballs through monopole condensations rather than volume-dependent fugacities. We investigate the k-SPUC (k-strong shortest path union cover) problem, which involves finding the fewest number of shortest paths needed to connect all nodes in a given graph. Our focus is on determining whether this problem can be solved efficiently for a limited set of graph configurations and establishing the minimum number of path selections required to achieve full coverage. We examine various graph types and demonstrate that the k-SPUC problem has a computationally complex classification (NP-complete) when applied to directed weighted graphs. By studying the infrared brightness of these clusters, I searched for microquasars, which could indicate the presence of alien biological signals. Since star-forming regions and young stellar populations like those found in open clusters are the most plausible targets for assessing panspermia, I focused on clusters containing early-type main-sequence stars with spectral types O to F. To minimize contamination from background sources, I restricted the sample to clusters with well-defined half-mass radii and low stellar densities. Using the Spitzer data, I probed a distance of up to 10 half-mass radii from the cluster center and analyzed the infrared brightness distribution within this area. For each cluster, I identified the brightest infrared sources and assessed their likelihood of being real stars, and then searched for signs of microquasars. Although no conclusive alien signals were found, the study offers a framework for exploring panspermia and encourages further investigation with more sensitive telescopes. The analysis also provides a method for distinguishing artificial signals from real stars and sheds light on the characteristics of the stellar environments most suitable for evaluating panspermia, which are typically low-density areas like open star clusters. Researchers studying the spread of diseases within complex networks have recently discovered a significant phenomenon: a sudden increase in epidemic prevalence occurs near a critical point of a network's local connectivity transition. This phenomenon was initially observed in highly connected hub-and-spoke networks and is now being investigated in more general contexts. To further understand this phenomenon, researchers propose a new measure called "delocalized node attack" that focuses on removing nodes with the strongest connections to those with the fewest. By applying this measure, researchers conducted simulations to study the spread of diseases within various networks and found that the increased prevalence is caused by a phase transition in the network's local connectivity. Near this critical point, a significant amount of time is required for the epidemic to die out and the prevalence to decrease. This is demonstrated in simulations of the SIR model on different networks. However, the relationship between the epidemic prevalence and local connectivity near the critical point is highly dependent on the network structure and can vary significantly. Therefore, understanding these variations is essential for making accurate predictions about the spread of diseases within complex networks. 

This study introduces a new concept called "local coherency" which can be used to classify networks based on their structure during a transition phase. There are three main types of networks during this phase: (1) hub-and-spoke networks with high delocalized components, (2) tree-like networks with low delocalized components, and (3) self-similar networks with intermediate delocalized components. The delocalized component of a network can be effectively measured by the ratio of its second-highest shortest path length to its average shortest path length. This new measure provides valuable insights for understanding the spread of diseases within complex networks and can be applied to other processes that exhibit critical behavior and depend on local connectivity. 

In this study, the relationship between epidemic prevalence and local connectivity near a critical point was investigated in various networks, including power-law, Apollonian, and doped-fractal networks. The results show that a significant increase in epidemic prevalence occurs only in highly connected hub-and-spoke networks, while in self-similar networks with intermediate delocalized components, the prevalence increases more gradually and is influenced by the minimum of the power-law distribution of shortest path lengths. In contrast, in tree-like networks with low delocalized components, the prevalence increases more rapidly and is almost independent of the power-law distribution.

A search for the rare decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ e^-$ was conducted using data from Belle and Belle II. Since this decay involves muons in the final state, it's resistant to background from irradiation, making it an interesting objective for future experiments like CLAS12 and LHCb with upgraded detectors. Although no evidence was found, the current limit on branching fraction from this study has been significantly tightened to $4.0 \times 10^{-18}$, a more stringent restriction than previous reports. Additionally, the first measurement of the differential branchinng fraction in relation to dimuon invariant mass was made, showing the decay's likelihood decreases as the dimuon mass increases. Furthermore, the most precise estimation to date of the $\Sigma^-$ decay mode $\Sigma^- \to n \mu^+ e^-$ was also determined, with a branching fraction limit of $8.0 \times 10^{-19}$. In the case of $\Sigma^0$, the decay mode $ \Sigma^0 \to \gamma \mu^+ e^-$ remains unconstrained, however a limit on the decay mode $\Sigma^0 \to \mu^+ e^+ \pi^0 \pi^0$ was set at $4.3 \times 10^{-18}$. The study employed events from Belle (976 pb$^{-1}$, run from 1999 to 2008) and Belle II (2018 data, 48 pb$^{-1}$), with a muon momentum range between 6.5 GeV and 20 GeV and additional selection criteria to minimize background. The results were verified through two independent methods, with a zero signal contamination confirmed in both cases. The most precise limit on the decay mode $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ e^-$ was obtained using an enhanced dimuon mass resolution at Belle II. The research has the capacity to be enhanced by a factor of at least 25 in the case of Belle II and 100 in the case of future experiments like CLAS12 and LHCb with upgraded detectors. PILE consistently perform better than baseline techniques and are particularly effective

Quantum annealing is an algorithmic approach to solving combinatorial optimization problems and is being explored for its potential to lead to efficient solution of NP-complete issues. This study investigates how quantum annealing is impacted by two factors: a non-unity success probability and a finite decoherence time. We demonstrate that decoherence and time have a complex effect on quantum annealing's success, influencing it in a way that depends on the structure of the target Hamiltonian and the dynamics of the system during execution. Furthermore, we find that decoherence can have an unexpected effect - it can cause the probability of achieving the target ground state to decrease, not increase, leading to non-monotonic behavior. This effect is linked to the presence of intermediate states that are overcooked and result in suboptimal solutions. We also find that implementing a delay can sometimes improve success probability. Notably, this counterintuitive behavior is related to the presence of these intermediate states that are spoiled by decoherence and can be avoided by increasing the duration of quantum annealing or introducing a delay, demonstrating that quantum annealing can be improved through the management of these states. Additionally, we propose a related reason why quantum annealing might be resistant to thermal errors. Finally, we test and validate our findings using quantum annealing on a simulator and an actual machine. The experimental results from the simulator and the actual machine also exhibit the predicted non-monotonic behavior. The findings of this study offer novel insights into the behavior of quantum annealing and suggest possible avenues for improving its performance. The study indicates that the algorithm's success can be influenced by a complex interplay of parameters, including the structure of the target Hamiltonian, the dynamics of the system during execution, and the presence of decoherence. The findings also suggest that quantum annealing can be sensitive to thermal errors caused by decoherence, and that implementing a delay can be an effective strategy for improving its success, likely due to the destruction of intermediate states that are responsible for the failure to achieve the target ground state. The proposed explanation for quantum annealing's resistance to thermal errors provides a new perspective on this phenomenon and suggests that thermal stability is crucial for the algorithm's success. The findings of this study can be used to improve the performance of quantum annealing and may have implications for the development of other quantum algorithms that are also susceptible to thermal errors. The fact that the experimental results from the simulator and the actual machine exhibit the predicted non-monotonic behavior validates the theoretical findings of this study and confirms the existence of the proposed effect

This algorithm divides the training process into two phases: first, a smaller model is fine-tuned using localized examples; second, the model is adapted to incorporate additional modules, with the exception of the core component. The efficient model is then obtained through an efficient transfer process. This efficient model serves as a critic during the main training phase, allowing for the optimization of the entire network. Results have shown that this algorithm achieves comparable performance when compared to traditional training methods, with a significant reduction in training time. These complex simulations can be broken down into smaller, manageable components using a method called spatial decomposition. By doing so, the time it takes to run the simulation on supercomputers is significantly reduced, making it possible to use genetic algorithms for real-time damage detection. This algorithm works by randomly trying different solutions to a problem and selecting the one that seems most effective, which helps to pinpoint the location and severity of damage within the material. To function properly, the simulation needs to be precisely calibrated to mimic the actual behavior of the material under stress. When this is achieved, the algorithm can accurately identify even the smallest imperfections, such as delaminations, by comparing the simulated and actual acoustic patterns. To increase detection speed and accuracy across various loading conditions, it is necessary to run multiple simulations with different stress scenarios. By doing so, the algorithm can locate areas of the material that are prone to damage and prioritize further investigation. Due to its ability to adapt to new stress scenarios and refine its results, this intelligent material detection system represents a major advance in the field. Despite its promising future, further research is needed to apply this technology to real-world scenarios. Additionally, there are potential issues with the algorithm becoming stuck in local maxima, which could result from the random nature of the finite difference method. To mitigate this risk, it is necessary to implement a diverse range of starting conditions to ensure the most accurate solution is found. To validate this method, simulations were compared to actual experiments conducted on composite materials with various levels of damage. By refining the algorithm and conducting multiple trials, it was possible to achieve a high degree of accuracy in detecting even the smallest areas of damage. To take this technology a step further, it would be beneficial to incorporate machine learning into the simulation to enable it to adapt to new materials and stress scenarios more quickly. Despite the growth of learning-based control techniques, they often struggle with generalizability due to relying on simulation or being data-starved. To overcome this limitation, we've developed an approach that uses real-world experimentation to refine its own control method. We tested this approach on a complex scenario requiring multiple trials and demonstrated its effectiveness, outperforming traditional reinforcement learning methods despite using significantly less data. Furthermore, our approach successfully evolved a optimal solution for a different problem after just a few trials. We've applied our method to the challenging task of controlling a robot arm and achieved impressive results, with just 10 hours of experimentation yielding a highly accurate grasp. We've also shown that our approach can adapt to changes in its environment by evolving a robust grasp able to accommodate various objects and arm configurations. Our code is available at https://github.com/ashleyjwang/realworldrl.

We present an innovative approach to proving an integral identity by employing geometric vectors. This method not only yields a well-known identity but may also provide a novel perspective on an established result. Additionally, it seems that this approach has the potential to be a useful technique for tackling other complex problems. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we use it to derive a well-known formula for the area of an ellipse. Furthermore, we explore the potential of this approach to be applied to a broader range of curves and surfaces. To do this, we consider an arbitrary differentiable curve defined by parametric equations and examine how our approach can be adapted to it. Finally, we provide a formula for calculating the area of a curve as an alternative to the usual approach using parametric integration. This new approach leads to an interesting observation about the relationship between line and space vectors, which results in a more compact expression for the area of a curve. This new expression reveals a crucial aspect of the curve's geometry and may have a useful implications. This led to a more fundamental realization about the potential of geometric vectors to facilitate the computation of geometric quantities. This work is intended to provide a starting point for delving into vector calculus through geometric vectors and to encourage a more innovative approach to standard problems. It also aims to provide a unique perspective on well-known results and a starting point for exploring more intricate curves and surfaces. Then, we establish a connection between these identities and the higher-spin symmetry of the Wess-Zumino-Witten model based on $so(8)$, which reduces to the $SU(3)$ Toda conformal field theory through a degeneration limit. We determine the explicit form of the spin-three current in the $SU(3)$ Toda conformal field theory and verify that it satisfies the Virasoro algebra with central charge two. By employing this method, we explicitly reconstruct a wide class of twist fields for the Ising model and the $Z_3$ parafermion field theory, which agree with previously obtained results derived through the bosonization method. We offer a new, streamlined proof that uniform lattices correspond to bi-automatic groups. Our approach builds on the initial findings related to bi-automaticity among lattices and expands on the geometric method of proving group bi-automacity. Furthermore, our approach facilitates the extension of this result to the context of locally uniform lattices within higher-rank Grassmannians. Additionally, we outline a novel application of this method to demonstrate bi-automacity for certain uniform lattices within complex hyperbolic space. Lastly, we explore the potential for our approach to be used in settings of higher-dimensional locally symmetric spaces.

Computing the entropy of a probability distribution is a fundamental task, yet many distributions pose significant challenges due to their inherently complex nature. Certain distributions, such as those that depend on unseen parameters, cannot be directly evaluated and thus require special entropy estimation techniques. Even if a distribution can be directly evaluated, its entropy might still be computationally expensive to estimate accurately. To address these issues, this paper introduces three novel entropy approximation methods, leveraging techniques from functional programming to provide concise and efficient solutions. These methods are applicable to a broad range of continuous univariate probability distributions, including those with unseen parameters. We demonstrate the efficacy of our methods with two cost models, showing they outperform existing methods by significant factors in terms of computational speed and memory usage. Moreover, we exhibit the practical usefulness of our methods by applying them to real-world data analysis scenarios within the Scala programming environment. Our methods are implemented as a type-class framework and made available as part of the Scala general-purpose statistics library, Scala-Stats. This library is open-source and can be accessed via the GitHub repository at https://github.com/aleksejpondik/scala-stats. A standalone implementation of our entropy approximation methods is also included as part of the Scala-Stats repository at https://github.com/aleksejpondik/scala-stats-entropies. Dynamic graph classification is a challenging task due to the significant changes that occur within graph structures over time. Most existing methods primarily focus on static graph analysis and fail to capture the temporal evolution of graph connections. To address this issue, we introduce the DECENNT model, a deep learning approach that utilizes temporal evolution information to enhance the representation of dynamic graphs. By converting time-dependent adjacency matrices into unique initial node representations, our model leverages structural information along the temporal dimension. The study of particle movement is commonly analyzed using mean squared displacement as a metric of diffusion. However, this approach typically assumes a uniform diffusion rate across the observation period. In reality, particles with controlled movement may exhibit changing diffusion rates, while living entities are subject to additional constraints such as speed limits and preferred movement directions. By examining the time series of these constraints, we found that the conventional mean squared displacement method often fails to distinguish between living and non-living particles. To address this shortcoming, we developed a statistical test to determine whether the diffusion rate varies over time and a new metric called the fractional integrated variance, which takes into account the shape of the diffusion rate distribution. By applying these methods to simulated data and actual cell trail images, we found that the new approach successfully identifies living particles and provides a more accurate measurement of their movement characteristics. Additionally, we found that the new metric can differentiate between different diffusion processes. Our study offers novel statistical tools that enhance our ability to analyze particle movement and provide valuable insights into the complex systems from which the data originate. Furthermore, our model was also applied to study how the composition of stress fibers changes in response to changes in cellular forces and how this affects their mechanical properties. The principles of this multi-filament model can also be applied to other bundled filaments found within cells and the extracellular matrix. The agent observes the context and receives the recommended action, but its ability to communicate with the manager is restricted. We investigate two communication protocols: the manager sends the context to the agent, which then chooses an action and informs the manager of the reward; and the agent chooses an action based on a provided context and receives the corresponding reward, then informs the manager. To minimize the expected communication cost, we develop a linear regression-based approach for the first protocol and a non-parametric low-pass filter method for the second protocol. We investigated the large-scale behavior of wireless networks with power-controlled transmission, comparing binary and optimal power control under a mean power constraint. Our analysis focused on a general non-fading scenario and one specific fading type - namely, independent and identically distributed block-fading with two states. Our results showed that, in the non-fading case, binary power control performs only slightly worse than optimal power control, with a roughly 50% loss in throughput. In contrast, for the fading case, binary power control performs significantly worse, with a loss of nearly a logarithm of the number of users. However, this large loss can be achieved without knowledge of the network load. Our findings also revealed that, when the fading is independent and identically distributed across users, the performance difference between binary and optimal power control is largely unaffected. Finally, our results include various simulations to verify our theoretical findings. This paper proposes a feedback control system for a robotic hopping mechanism that can quickly adapt to various terrain conditions, including soft ground. Furthermore, the feedback control system was found to maintain the robotic hopper's desired hop height, even on soft ground. The proposed feedback control system can potentially be applied to the development of bio-inspired robots that navigate through air and on various ground surfaces. The associated nonlinear model and feedback control law are also applicable to other robotic hopping mechanisms that adhere to the same design principles. We introduce the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), a novel Bayesian model, as a tool for analyzing complex information networks and identifying relevant topics. This model builds upon the Dirichlet Multinomial Mixtures (DMM) topic model by incorporating a hierarchical structure and utilizing document-specific topic distributions. We demonstrate that DMM can be viewed as a special instance of HDTM, enabling the application of established inference methods. Furthermore, the hierarchical nature of HDTM enables the extraction of topic hierarchies, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the data. Although the competitive posterior is complex and multi-modal, we leverage the coupling between document topics and the hierarchical structure to constrain the space of possible solutions, facilitating effective exploration. As a result, our model performs better than alternative models in topic discovery tasks and can produce coherent topic hierarchies. To facilitate the use of HDTM in large datasets, we develop an efficient variational inference method based on the alternating proximal gradient technique. We evaluate the model on three real-world datasets, including Wikipedia and arXiv, and show that it outperforms other topic models. Additionally, the extracted topic hierarchies are displayed and found to be accurate and informative. As the model's complexity increases with the size of the dataset, we recommend using the Hierarchical Document Topic Model for medium-sized datasets consisting of up to 10,000 documents. As the model can be viewed as a generalization of DMM, we expect it to be applicable to any dataset that can be treated as documents. Consequently, the model may be useful for analyzing information networks in science citation fields and web pages. Quantum annealing, a method for solving combinatorial optimization problems, faces a challenge in efficiently transitioning between states during its execution. This phenomenon, where the system becomes trapped in a local minimum due to mismatched annealing and decay times, is known as the annealing gap. Determining the duration of this gap, which varies depending on the system and problem being solved, could inform the development of improved quantum annealing protocols, such as those that gradually increase the decay rate or incorporate periodic resets. Using a new simulation tool that combines classical and quantum time-evolution, we were able to study the annealing gap in detail for the example problem of a Ising model implemented using both qubit-based quantum annealing and continuous-variable quantum annealing. This allowed us to investigate the impact of different decoherence rates, as well as the properties of the system and its driver, on the annealing gap. Furthermore, we examined the effectiveness of several decay-rate modulation strategies in overcoming the annealing gap. While these protocols can sometimes succeed in avoiding the annealing gap, our findings suggest that they may have limitations and may not always be beneficial. Instead, we propose a simple criterion for determining when a given protocol will become stuck due to the annealing gap and suggest the potential for improving quantum annealing by optimizing this criterion through the careful design of the driver and interaction terms. This could potentially lead to better performance in experiments that account for decoherence. Additionally, we observed that the behavior of quantum annealing can sometimes be understood through the application of classical analogs, such as the random walk, and that the success or failure of certain protocols may depend on whether the system transitions between states in a continuous or discrete manner. The insights gained from this research could be used to inform the development of other quantum optimization protocols that face similar challenges. The techniques employed in this study are highly versatile and can be readily applied to the examination of other quantum systems and protocols. The tools developed for this research also provide a framework for investigating other phenomena, such as the interplay between decoherence and annealing in systems that exhibit multiple metastable states. The simulation framework used in this research is also capable of accurately modeling the behavior of quantum systems in situations where both classical and quantum time-evolution descriptions yield significantly different results. Inertial wave turbulence was initially proposed by Balenda et al. to be self-similar, 
and this study confirms that theory. The resulting spectrum matches the one derived 
by Valivita and Manhaeve for rotating rectangular containers. Additionally, this 
self-similarity is observed in a new context - within a container with multiple 
obstacles, as evidenced by the matching of our measured and modelled spectra. 
Our findings also offer a method for accurately estimating the amplitude of 
inertial wave turbulence. Our unique experimental setup allows for the generation 
of both localized and sustained turbulent states, achieved by dropping objects of 
varying mass into different regions of a rotating cylinder filled with water. Our 
results demonstrate that the spectrum of inertial wave turbulence is unaffected 
by either the amplitude of the turbulence or its initial conditions. Our results 
may have implications for understanding self-similar behavior in other complex 
systems.

We propose an easily adaptable semi-supervised medical image segmentation technique, utilizing interpolation-based mixing. This method leverages a common characteristic of interpolation methods - reducing noise - to devise a data augmentation strategy. By combining unlabeled images with shifted versions of a limited, high-quality labeled dataset, it regularizes the model. This approach simplifies the complex interactions between different interpolation methods and gradient descent optimizers, allowing for efficient model training. Compared to an accurate but time-consuming baseline method, our proposed technique achieves comparable performance on the LIDC-IDRI dataset (with 1000 annotations) and significantly outperforms the baseline on a dataset with only 100 annotations. Additionally, it demonstrates versatility by successfully applying the technique to a different modality and anatomy (colon vs. chest computed tomography). The code is openly accessible on https://github.com/TraversedMM/SSGM. By streamlining the process and yielding satisfactory results, this method provides an accessible solution for semi-supervised medical image segmentation.

This paper examines the implications of using weak convergence to estimate functions of parameters that satisfy certain regularity conditions, specifically those defined by the concept of estimable functions. Our analysis indicates that the rate of weak convergence can vary depending on whether the underlying model involves a single parameter or multiple parameters. In the case of a single parameter, we demonstrate that consistent estimates can achieve a rate of convergence of $n^{-1/2}$, even if the model includes a nonidentifiable component. On the other hand, we show that under certain conditions, weak convergence at a rate of $n^{-1/2}-\log n$ can be achieved for estimates of parameters that define probability measures on $\mathbb{R}^d$, provided that the true parameter values are separated from the set of nonidentifiable parameters. When there are multiple parameters, we establish a result indicating that the rate of weak convergence can be aspired but may not be achievable in general. Instead, we derive a non-asymptotic result that provides a lower bound for the rate of weak convergence. Furthermore, we explore conditions under which the optimal rate of weak convergence can be achieved for specific cases of statistical models, including multivariate normal models and models that involve a single location parameter. Our findings are validated through simulations and real-world applications. Notably, we provide an adaptation of the standard cross-validation procedure to estimate the optimal bandwidth, which can be applied across a broad spectrum of statistical models. This method, which we refer to as the 'generalized cross-validation', can be employed across various models, including those that involve multiple parameters. Our results highlight the superiority of this method over alternative approaches in a certain context. Additionally, our work leads to an interesting theoretical result that may have implications for deriving the optimal rate of weak convergence in models with multiple parameters. Lastly, our study paves the way for further research on the convergence rate of estimators in statistical models with complex structures. 

This work is relevant to several ongoing research projects that aim to address challenges related to nonidentifiable parameters in statistical models. It is hoped that our findings will contribute to a greater understanding of the methods used to overcome these challenges and, ultimately, lead to the development of more effective strategies for estimating complex statistical models.

The field of node embedding has seen a recent surge in new algorithms developed to capture complex graph structures. Unfortunately, most of these novel approaches lack rigorous testing and are not suitable for broad use. This paper introduces a critical framework for assessing node embedding algorithms and applies it to a range of methods, including both classical and cutting-edge techniques. By utilizing the framework, we identify key factors that influence performance and examine the embeddability of different graphs. Our results demonstrate that existing algorithms become ineffective for certain complex graph types, thereby highlighting a clear gap in current understanding. To address this, we introduce multiple new evaluation metrics and node embedding scenarios to provide a comprehensive framework for criticizing and comparing node embedding algorithms. By utilizing our proposed framework, we conduct an in-depth analysis of two representative algorithms, namely DeepWalk and GCN, and reveal their limitations when dealing with large and dense graphs, respectively. To bridge this gap, we introduce two novel node embedding algorithms, named LEA-GAN and LEA-ConD, which leverage complementary approaches like adversarial training and conditional construction to tackle distinct challenges. As a result, our work offers a thorough critique and comprehensive framework for evaluating node embedding algorithms, along with two innovative solutions to address specific challenges. This marks a significant step towards developing more effective and flexible node embedding algorithms. We introduce an innovative algorithm to accurately measure force in series elastic actuators, addressing difficulties caused by nonlinear material behavior and sensor inaccuracies. A key challenges in measuring force involves capturing the elastic actuator's complex stress-strain relationship. Another issue is sensing the position of the actuator's deformable end, which can be difficult to model precisely. These challenges lead to significant errors in estimating force based on sensor data alone. Our algorithm overcomes these limitations by using feedback from the sensor to estimate the current stress and therefore the corresponding force, without needing to model the actuator's material properties or its geometric shape. This approach leverages Kalman filter enhancements to improve its performance. Our method was tested on a physical setup consisting of an elastic actuator connected to a rigid link attached to the end of the deformable link. Results show our algorithm to be highly effective in accurately measuring force even in the presence of substantial nonlinearities and sensor errors. We explore a class of exact relativistic stellar models that consist of two interacting fluids, where one profile can be derived from a similar single-fluid model with a specific relation between the fluid parameters. This connection indicates that any single-fluid solution can be converted into a two-fluid solution, and the converse is also possible. The two-fluid solution is then a composite of the single-fluid solution and the interaction term. The interaction term's stress-energy tensor must satisfy certain constraints, which define the space of possible solutions. The two-fluid framework can thus be seen as the union of various single-fluid solutions, each representing a distinct approach to modeling the same interactions within the stars. Furthermore, the two-fluid solution allows for the exploration of phenomena related to the interaction terms in the relativistic stars, such as gravitational waves and the stability of these stars in various environments. The framework's potential also reveals that any single-fluid solution can be viewed as a specific two-fluid solution, where one fluid's interaction term vanishes. The two-fluid framework provides new avenues for modeling relativistic stars in multiple scenarios. The framework is particularly relevant for the study of stars with two interacting fluids in the context of general relativity and its extensions. The paper presents a general approach to deriving two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts and highlights the potential of the two-fluid framework to shed light on various phenomena involving interactions in relativistic stars. The effect of magnetic fields on the formation of merger remnants is being investigated by running sophisticated computer simulations. These simulations simulate the collision of two galaxy cores with rich gas supplies, similar in size to the Milky Way, under various conditions. The results indicate that magnetic fields can hinder the formation of merger remnants by limiting the formation of magnetic reconnection layers, which are crucial for converting magnetic energy back into heat and kinetic energy. Instead, magnetic fields become increasingly entangled during these collisions, leading to greater resistance to subsequent mergers. If magnetic fields are highly entangled initially, simulations show that magnetic fields may even repel each other, making it more difficult for galaxy cores to merge. However, if magnetic fields are weaker and more disorderly, they may facilitate the merger of galaxy cores. The implications of these findings are significant, as they suggest that magnetic fields may have a substantial impact on the growth of massive galaxies. Furthermore, the behavior of magnetic fields may influence the formation of low-metallic gas in galaxy collisions and, as a result, the creation of low-metallic gas in the universe. In addition, the results of these simulations provide valuable insights into the characteristics of magnetic fields in galaxy collisions and how they evolve over time. The findings also suggest that magnetic fields play a significant role in shaping the magnetic fields of galaxy cores and their magnetic fields' impact on the formation of merger remnants. This model incorporates two key components: a contrastive training method using Mixup technique and a 3D segmentation network. Recent studies have achieved significant progress in Generalizing to Error Types (GEC) using neural models, however most of these models are only adaptable to a limited range of errors and their performance significantly degrades when confronted with unfamiliar errors. This phenomenon restricts their generalization to various types of GEC, such as spell checking and sentence correction. To address this issue, this work adapts neural GEC models through a method that learns from data that contains different error types, without needing the explicit definitions of those error types. This proposed adaptation method is based on a modified version of the neural model that is trained in an unsupervised manner to identify shared knowledge between the source and target data, and is compared to other GEC adaptation techniques. The results show that this method significantly outperforms traditional multi-task transfer learning approaches and other adaptation methods, especially when adapting to more distant error types. For example, when adapting a model trained on sentence correction to spell checking, the proposed method achieves a higher F-score (+2.9%) compared to the baseline model that is trained from scratch (+11.6%). This work demonstrates the ability of neural GEC models to generalize to various types of errors and produces models that can effectively deal with unfamiliar errors, making them more suitable for real-world applications. Moreover, this work proposes a new evaluation metric called Max F-score at N, which indicates the model's performance when adapting to the Nth error type, and provides the implementation of the proposed adaptation method in the Generalizing to Error Types dataset. This work also highlights the challenges posed by extremely rare error types, such as abbreviations and homonyms, that remain an open research problem in the GEC field. In 2020, Japan faced a severe emergency due to a nationwide suicide cluster, a coronavirus-related mental health crisis exacerbated by the pandemic. To mitigate this crisis, the Japanese government hastily rounded certain suicide statistics, obscuring actual suicide data. This study uses actual suicide numbers to explore the effects of rounding on statistical analysis, particularly on rate estimates, confidence intervals, and standardized rate ratios. It also investigates how the method of data discretization, namely single-year vs. five-year intervals, influences these analyses. Additionally, suicide rate trends before the crisis were factored into the analysis to assess how the crisis influenced different population groups. Our findings highlight the difficulties of accurately interpreting data that has been intentionally obscured, as witnessed in the recent Japanese suicide cluster crisis. Furthermore, we emphasize the significance of preserving precise data in order to facilitate thorough analysis and informed decision-making. Our research also offers novel methods for conducting statistical analyses on a limited, aggregated dataset. Ultimately, we stress the need for transparent data presentation to avoid misleading inferences and to effectively tackle pressing public health issues. This study is an urgent response to the recent Japanese suicide cluster crisis; however, its findings have broader applicability to any scenario where data is intentionally obscured, as is evident in the recent Japanese suicide cluster crisis fueled by the pandemic. We present a thorough investigation of the GdInO3 crystal structure, a member of the AMO3 family, conducted via experimental and theoretical approaches. Experiments utilizing X-ray diffraction, EPR, and Mossbauer spectroscopy, along with heat capacity and magnetic measurements, reveal that GdInO3 exhibits a type of lattice where Gd+ ions are arranged in a hexagonal closed packing pattern and where the Gd+ and In+ ions are randomly distributed within the lattice sites. Conversely, Monte Carlo simulations and a Metropolis algorithm found that a random mixing of the Gd+ and In+ ions in a body-centered cubic lattice does not display the same level of magnetic ordering when compared to the actual GdInO3 system. Nevertheless, the simulated systems exhibit a spin freezing transition similar to the one observed in the actual GdInO3 compound. The results of the heat capacity measurements also confirm the presence of a spin freezing transition in the GdInO3 system. The estimated value of the exchange interaction energy is found to be around 6.2 k_B, which is a product of the exchange interaction and the correlation between the adjacent spins. The observed spin freezing transition in the GdInO3 system is attributed to the disorder within the lattice. The results of the heat capacity measurements also indicate that the disorder within the lattice does not have any negative impact on the magnetic ordering, instead it enhances it. The estimated value of the energy barrier for the magnetic ordering is found to be around 23.2 k_B. The results of the Monte Carlo simulations and the heat capacity measurements suggest that the GdInO3 system may display magnetic order above the spin freezing temperature with an increased magnetic field. We examine the integration of two methods for allocating indivisible goods among discrete cycles of agents: the Round-Robin mechanism and the cut-and-choose algorithm. Fairness is assessed using the utilitarian and egalitarian norms, and we investigate how different combined approaches perform. Notably, when applying the mechanisms to cycle-free allocations obtained through the cut-and-choose algorithm, the Round-Robin method provides a fairer allocation under the egalitarian norm, although it may result in some unallocated goods. Conversely, using the cut-and-choose algorithm for cycle contents yields a more fair allocation under the utilitarian norm. However, integrating both methods may result in all goods being allocated. We also examine whether our proposed integrated frameworks can lead to fairer allocations compared to executing the mechanisms individually. Our findings indicate a diverse set of outcomes, dependent on the underlying allocation structure, and suggest that the efficacy of each method varies based on fairness norms and whether goods are allocated. Nonetheless, some combined approaches outperform executing the mechanisms separately, and we identify instances where doing so leads to a fairer allocation. Moreover, applying the mechanisms to specific types of cycle contents may yield fairer allocations, and we provide guarantees for specific fairness norms in those cases. These guarantees are fairer than $2/n$ under the egalitarian norm and $\Delta(a^*)/n$ under the utilitarian norm, where $a^*$ represents the optimal allocation for a given set of goods and agents. As a by-product, we establish a lower bound of $1-\frac{1}{e}$ (approximately 0.63) on the expected cyclic fair share for an arbitrary allocation of goods to a random cycle of $n$ agents. This finding provides a more precise guarantee than previous estimates and has a significant implication for comparing the expected cyclic fair share to individual fair shares in various cycles of agents. Additionally, our analysis highlights diverse internal structures within cycles of agents that may result in some agents having no interaction in economic trading processes. Lastly, our investigation paves the way for further exploration of the interplay between economic trading processes and cycle structures. As an illustrative example, our findings on the round-robin mechanism for allocating goods among cycles of agents can be extended to a trading process where an agent offers goods to a cycle of other agents, and the round-robin mechanism is applied to determine the allocation among the cycle contents. We propose a novel approach to pseudo-labeling, which involves using multiple translations of the same target image to generate more reliable and diverse predictions. By averaging the predictions from these translations, we can reduce the impact of translation flaws and biases, ultimately producing better pseudo-targets. Since our approach requires a large number of diverse translations, we introduce an iterative strategy to pseudo-labelers, where earlier pseudo-targets are used to generate additional translations, which are then combined with the original set to produce even better pseudo-targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments, showing significant improvements over conventional pseudo-labeling methods. Notably, our approach achieves top-ranked performance on the ATEC benchmark dataset, surpassing other techniques by a substantial 1.6% in error rate. Additionally, our approach proves particularly effective at exploiting diverse translation styles (e.g., using different backbone networks), achieving a remarkable 5.4% decrease in error rate. Overall, our results highlight the potential of our approach to significantly enhance pseudo-labeling performance, making it an invaluable tool for efficiently acquiring a large amount of diverse and high-quality target data.

The galaxy UGC 8839, which resembles the Milky Way, has a ring structure and no prominent spiral arms. By utilizing wide-field narrowband imaging, we were able to identify over 130 HII regions within this galaxy. The detection of 91 HII regions in UGC 8839 allows for a comparison with 307 HII regions found in NGC 628. From this comparison, a distinct pattern emerges - HII regions in UGC 8839 are located at a significantly greater average distance from the galaxy's center (4.6 kpc) compared to those in NGC 628 (2.9 kpc). The distribution of HII regions in UGC 8839 is randomly dispersed across different galactocentric radii, whereas in NGC 628, HII regions are concentrated at specific radial ranges. By analyzing the relationship between the luminosity of HII regions and their radial distance from the galaxy's center, a trend is observed in both galaxies. However, UGC 8839 exhibits a more pronounced decrease in luminosity with increasing radial distance. The lower surface density of HII regions in UGC 8839, particularly in areas close to the galaxy's center, may be attributed to the presence of molecular gas reservoirs. The lower frequency of interacting HII regions in UGC 8839 (23%) is notable, with only a small portion of these interactions occurring with molecular clouds. The lower rate of interacting HII regions in UGC 8839 may contribute to its distinct HII region population distribution. By analyzing the relationship between the mass of bulge and disk in UGC 8839 and NGC 628 using HII regions as mass probes, we found no significant differences in mass density within these galaxies. However, UGC 8839 exhibits a more prominent bulge, which may be attributed to recent interactions with the giant low-surface-brightness spiral galaxy CVS 779. These interactions may have led to the transfer of bulge mass from UGC 8839 to CVS 779 and caused the ring structure in UGC 8839. The ring structure in UGC 8839 is thought to have originated from a major merger event. The distribution of HII regions in UGC 8839 supports computer simulations indicating that the galaxy has experienced recent interaction with a massive disk galaxy. The collision with this galaxy may have triggered the formation of the ring structure in UGC 8839. This work lays the groundwork for the creation of secure, confidential databases that balance user privacy with functional data management capabilities. Understanding how model performance is affected by individual features is crucial for automated debugging in machine learning. We investigate the concept of minimal unsatisfiable cores in the context of Boolean satisfiability testing-based automated debugging. By applying this core to a learning model, we can determine the interplay between the model and a set of data. The core's features that are in conflict with the model can be used to create new logical constraints that limit model flexibility. These constraints help pinpoint important features among those that have a significant impact on the model-performance data relationship. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by conducting experiments using both synthetic and real-world data. The results show that our approach can accurately identify important features and outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the performance of the model is improved when features that were previously unknown are added. The improved model achieves this performance boost without needing extensive hyperparameter tuning. The approach that we present can be used to create a new technique for machine learning feature selection known as Minimal Unsatisfiable Core-based Feature Selection. This approach addresses key challenges related to the scalability, robustness, and generalizability of current methods. The experiments that we conducted are also available online at https://github.com/parth17/mucs-ecs-2368-experiments. The accurate detection and segmentation of surgical instruments are crucial components in the development of supportive systems for minimally invasive surgery. To enhance tool detection, our research introduces the Dual decoder attention network (DDANet), which segments instruments from the start to the end of the procedure. We apply the DDANet to a new dataset containing the complete surgery on one ankle, achieving a remarkable 84.8% segmentation accuracy, outperforming other cutting-edge networks. When only observing a random 20% of the surgery, the DDANet's performance drops slightly to 68.2% accuracy. When trained on a much larger dataset containing the start of four surgeries, the DDANet exhibits an impressive 87.4% accuracy. Notably, our findings indicate that attention mechanisms play a key role in the success of the network. When incorporating an attention mechanism in the encoder layer, the network's performance increases from 75.5% to 84.8% accuracy when operating on the entire ankle surgery. Similarly, in the decoder layer, the attention mechanism boosts the accuracy from 68.4% to 84.8%. To facilitate further research, we introduce two novel metrics: the average accuracy of the largest instrument (AAli) and the accuracy of detecting any instrument (ADI). These metrics prove particularly useful in evaluating the success of instrument detection algorithms. Additionally, our work highlights significant challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable and accurate detection of surgical instruments across diverse and dynamic surgical environments. This includes developing more robust algorithms capable of accurately detecting instruments in low-light settings and in the presence of occlusions. Furthermore, there is a need for more data collection methods that can capture a wide range of procedures and settings to support the training of these algorithms. Ultimately, there is value in combining algorithmic approaches with human expertise and oversight to ensure the highest standards of safety and reliability. As a result, we recommend a combined human-algorithmic approach to enhancing surgical tool detection and developing more effective data collection methods that can capture a diverse range of procedures and settings. This will help address the challenges associated with the dynamic nature of surgical environments and facilitate the reliable deployment of surgical tool detection systems. Recently, deep learning techniques have significantly enhanced the matching efficiency of Re-identification (ReID) images. Nonetheless, building a robust ReID model without labeled data remains a significant challenge. To address this, we propose a contrastive learning-based unsupervised ReID method, dubbed CoFL, which incorporates cross-domain distillation to leverage the information from labeled datasets. By employing a contrastive loss on both the domain discrepancy and disentangled features, CoFL significantly boosts the matching performance. Moreover, CoFL introduces a novel cycle cross entropy loss to rectify the pose disentanglement, thereby achieving more accurate separations of pose and background. Comprehensive experiments on widely used ReID datasets, including MSMT27k and CUHK03, demonstrate that CoFL surpasses existing unsupervised ReID methods by delivering superior performance. Moreover, a comparison with supervised ReID approaches reveals that CoFL boasts competitive results. Ultimately, CoFL showcases great potential in exploiting unlabeled data to enhance the robustness of ReID models. Source code is available at: https://github.coFL-UCAS-ICT.

Recent advancements in machine learning, coupled with the emergence of powerful computational tools and vast financial data sets, have led to heightened interest in replacing conventional GARCH models with more sophisticated alternatives. While existing studies have utilized single models to forecast Value-at-Risk, the inherent diversity and unpredictability of stock market behavior suggests that a solitary model may not suffice. In response, we present an innovative ensemble of GARCH, LSTM, and GRU models that leverages the unique strengths of each component to provide a comprehensive and adaptable framework for VAR forecasting. Unlike existing hybrid approaches that rely on arbitrary linear combinations of model outputs, our proposed framework incorporates an enhanced feature-based extraction method that leverages pedagogical explanations of financial variables to capture their intricate dynamics. Furthermore, our approach transcends traditional limitations by incorporating an efficient model selection mechanism that identifies optimal components based on the minimization of loss functions. Empirical evaluations conducted across six major stock market indices reveal that our proposed framework not only outperforms fundamental GARCH models but also exhibits superior performance relative to individual LSTM and GRU models, showcasing the benefits of diverse structural features and dynamic temporal capabilities in VAR forecasting. Lastly, our framework's efficiency in model selection and feature extraction in relation to alternative hybrid approaches that rely on arbitrary linear combinations or exhaustive searches in model selection is highlighted. Ultimately, our results validate the potential of sophisticated machine learning models as viable alternatives to fundamental GARCH models for VAR forecasting applications. Moreover, our research provides valuable insights into the selection of optimal models for VAR forecasting, emphasizing the importance of considering various structural features and dynamic temporal capabilities to capture the intricate dynamics of stock market behavior. Ultimately, our approach provides a foundation for exploring other efficient model selection mechanisms that prioritize model diversity and minimal loss complexity. Moreover, our feature extraction method offers a framework for further interdisciplinary research that integrates financial theory and machine learning-based pedagogical explanations of financial variables. Lastly, our study's findings and model architecture are made readily available for replication and further exploration in related research projects. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/AbdullahAlDallal/Hybrid-VAR-forecasting. Our study's data is obtainable from Refinitiv (formerly Thomson Reuters) and our paper's detailed methodology, accompanying figures, and tables are openly available at https://osf.io/ycpbd.

We analyzed the sampling of pulsar timing array data using Gaussian processes and evaluated two probabilistic sampling methods, rejection sampling and a Markov chain Monte Carlo approach. We found that, while the Monte Carlo method was the most efficient, rejection sampling still effectively narrowed possible signal periods. However, due to the time-consuming nature of Monte Carlo simulations, rejection sampling proved valuable for preliminary screenings of data. Additionally, our results demonstrated that the two methods could be used in tandem to analyze a wider range of samples. By leveraging the faster rejection sampling for initial assessments and then switching to the more accurate Monte Carlo method for analysis, we were able to evaluate 10,000 to 100,000 samples in a matter of hours. This strategy allowed us to fully examine various pulsar combinations and search for localized signals over a broader frequency range. By comparing the two methods, we were able to determine the optimal sampling settings and identify potential limitations due to pulsar noise. Finally, our findings highlighted opportunities for enhancing sampling algorithms and integrating them with other analysis approaches. By combining sampling and the characteristics of pulsar data, we were able to identify key factors that influence signal detection and developed a framework for comparing sampling methods in this context. This led to valuable insights into the performance of sampling algorithms when analyzing pulsar timing array data. As a result of this research, the sample set that can be evaluated in a given computational time has been significantly increased, paving the way for more comprehensive analyses of pulsar data. This progress, in turn, may lead to the detection of localized gravitational waves and further understanding of pulsar behavior. This work was based on previous research into probabilistic approaches to analyzing pulsar timing array data and built upon existing implementations in the PyS4J package. This work not only further developed those algorithms but also demonstrated their value in practice. People generally agree that helping the less fortunate is important. However, whether it's acceptable to redistribute wealth when an individual's fortune is purely down to luck is a more contentious issue. Using a simple economic model, we examine how the perceived morality of luck-based wealth distribution affects public willingness to pay for a chance to avoid being randomly impoverished. Our results reveal that when luck determines opportunities rather than income, there's a significant surge in demand for this option. In contrast, people are largely indifferent when luck directly dictates their income. Interestingly, we find that the majority of respondents prioritize avoiding random poverty over the potential gain, despite it being a relatively small risk. Our findings also show that cultural norms influencing these preferences vary significantly. Further, we discovered that the value people place on avoiding luck-based hardship is notably higher when the stakes are lower, albeit ultimately remaining relatively stable. Notably, the relationship between risk aversion and these results holds true only when the probability of being affected is low, whereas it loses significance at higher risk levels. The non-detection of radio emission from known neutron star X-ray binaries located in the crowded environments of globular clusters poses a challenge for identifying whether any newly discovered radio sources within these clusters are actually millisecond pulsars or neutron star X-ray binaries. To address this issue, researchers have conducted thorough radio surveys of five core-rich globular clusters using the VLA. Their study has produced extensive lists of radio sources within these clusters, including four previously unknown radio sources found in the cores of four globular clusters: M15, M14, M5, and M13. By examining the positions of these sources in infrared images, the researchers were able to determine that three of these sources are likely front-side radio sources associated with first-generation pulsars or neutron star X-ray binaries, while the fourth source is a second-generation radio source likely associated with a millisecond pulsar. The researchers also found that the distribution of radio sources in the cores of these clusters follows a density profile indicative of hierarchical formation processes within these clusters. The non-detection of radio sources in the outer fields of these clusters suggests that any neutron star X-ray binaries located in the outer fields of these clusters may not be interacting with their clusters' stellar populations. The non-detection of front-side radio sources in the outer fields of these clusters suggests that any front-side radio sources in these regions may not be associated with pulsars or neutron star X-ray binaries. The researchers estimate that up to 25 neutron star X-ray binaries may remain undetected in the outer fields of these five clusters. The discovery of a variable X-ray source near a front-side radio source in M14 may indicate that this X-ray source is a 1.7-second X-ray pulsar. The researchers propose that future observations of these radio sources and potential X-ray sources in these clusters with highly sensitive radio and X-ray telescopes like the VLA, the EVLA, the Chandra, the XMM-Newton, the NuSTAR, the future Square Kilometre Array, and the future Generation X/XO/XC telescopes may reveal more neutron star X-ray binaries and pulsars in these clusters. The researchers also highlight the importance of comparing the properties of these front-side radio sources with those of the second-generation radio sources found in the cores of these clusters in order to gain insights into the formation and evolution of these clusters. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of using high-resolution radio surveys to identify front-side radio sources associated with pulsars or neutron star X-ray binaries in the crowded environments of globular clusters

Despite being straightforward to execute, these tests can provide valuable insights into the performance of these gates. This protocol proposes utilizing the toric code - a well-known topological code - as a comprehensive benchmark to evaluate the combined efficacy of multiple gates. We outline a reduced set of gate tests that are equivalent in benchmarking capability to evaluating the entanglement between adjacent sites within the toric code model. Additionally, we examine the minimum number of tests required to achieve a specific level of error threshold when diagnosing faulty gate operations. Our results demonstrate that just three of these tests can sufficiently determine the error probability with which the code's stability is threatened. Furthermore, we investigate the constraints imposed by both classical and quantum versions of the Simon theorem on the minimal number of tests required. Our findings indicate that, in the case of classical diagnostics, the smallest number of tests needed to determine any error threshold strictly increases with the number of error thresholds examined. This paper introduces a novel, efficient method for adapting Lloyd's clustering approach that utilizes feedback information from a limited number of pilot transmissions. Unlike traditional Lloyd's algorithm, our proposed method takes into account the distortion caused by transmitting data to a cluster instead of treating each data point individually. We demonstrate that our approach offers significantly reduced pilot requirements compared to conventional methods. In particular, if the number of clusters is set to $K$, our method achieves a substantial decrease of around $K^{2d}$ in pilot requirements over Lloyd's algorithm, where $d$ represents the dimensionality of the data. Furthermore, our proposed method has a comparable computational complexity to Lloyd's algorithm. Through various experiments, we show that our method not only reduces pilot requirements but also provides similar compression performance to Lloyd's algorithm. The benefits of our approach are especially notable in high-dimensional data sets. We also evaluate our method in real-world scenarios with real data sets and find that it yields competitive results. In this design, successful bids are either fully executed and count towards the final clearing price, or they fail to clear and do not contribute to the price. Furthermore, the proposed design is shown to reduce volatility and prices across all levels of generation and consumption. The results also indicate that the grid operator's orders exhibit greater consistency in responding to changes in independent power operators' behavior under the all-or-none design. The model is validated through collaboration with control room managers and supervisors from four European transmission system operators, yielding valuable market design recommendations. The suggested 'all-or-none' design is deemed feasible and efficient for redispatch markets and is proposed for adoption in conjunction with existing price-based mechanisms. We investigate the quantum mechanical properties of a particular film structure made from Tellurene and a related material Tellurene-oxide, examining both their quantum well and quantum wire forms. By manipulating the strain applied to these structures, we are able to achieve a significant non-trivial gap that could make them useful for applications in photodetectors and optoelectronics. Quantum spin Hall phases also emerge in these structures at appropriate strain levels. The most suitable strain levels vary depending on the material used, but a Tellurene-oxide film shows great potential due to its stability and ease of production. A semi-empirical tight-binding model can be applied to these oxide films, allowing us to predict their electronic properties and suggest relevant experimental research should be conducted. Furthermore, we identify the optimal strain levels that would bring about a substantial non-trivial gap in both well and wire forms. These predictions position these oxide films as promising materials for use in quantum spin Hall devices. Additionally, we propose that these materials could be used as functional layers in the improvement of tunneling current in tunnel field effect transistors. The introduced concept of strain engineering opens up new possibilities for the control of electronic and optical properties in these materials, bringing us closer to the development of reliable and efficient Tellurene-based devices.

The backpropagation algorithm, though effective, relies on computationally costly matrix operations and extensive memory allocation. To circumvent these limitations, we explore an alternative training method based on physical analogies, specifically the Adjoint Algorithm, which utilizes electrical analog circuits to replicate neural network components and learn from data. We demonstrate the feasibility of using the Adjoint Algorithm for weight update by investigating a simplified case where the error is directly applied to resistors in a circuit, thus evading the need for costly matrix computations. Moreover, our proposed method offers a notable reduction in training time and energy consumption compared to traditional backpropagation. To realize this approach, we examine the concept of analog computing and examine the limitations and potential pitfalls when implementing the Adjoint Algorithm. Finally, we discuss the challenges and requirements for scaling this method to more complex neural network architectures. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves significant speed-ups and energy efficiency on large-scale neural network applications. However, our approach faces a major bottleneck due to the limited scalability of analog components, leading to a significant hurdle in implementing large-scale neural networks using this method. Still, we believe that with the advancement of analog computing technology and innovative system architectures, the Adjoint Algorithm holds great promise for efficient deep learning. To move forward, we suggest integrating multiple small-scale analog modules to create a hybrid system that can learn efficiently. We also highlight potential research directions for the community to explore and address technical limitations and open questions. These proposals could pave the way for reevaluating analog computing and the Adjoint Algorithm in deep learning applications. We introduce a one-dimensional mixed opinion formation model, where both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions are present, and examine how these interactions affect the average magnetization. By comparing it to the same calculation for an isolated Ising model, we find that the difference is actually how the two types of interactions contribute to the overall magnetization. Furthermore, we observe that the long-term behavior of the model can exhibit both ordered and disordered states, and we obtained the exact temperatures at which the phase transitions occur. Additionally, we obtained the exact values of the surface and bulk magnetization. For surface and bulk spins with different interactions, we derived explicit formulas for the order-disorder phase transitions. For the case where the interactions for the surface, bulk, and middle spins are all the same, we derived the exact values of the transition temperature through analytical derivation, and found that it corresponds to the $n=2$ universality class of Ising model phase transitions. By conducting Monte Carlo simulations, we verified our theoretical findings and observed the same ordering temperatures. We also found that the spin-flip and heat-bath update algorithms produce very similar results. Moreover, we found that for finite-size systems, the difference between these two update algorithms can be as high as 1% but generally converges to almost the same result with only a few exceptions. We also found that for some specific temperatures and spin flip update, the magnetization becomes stuck in local minima and cannot achieve the same level of ordering as seen with the heat-bath algorithm. We argue that this phenomenon may indicate that some algorithms are capable of distinguishing between the thermodynamic state and metastable states. We propose that this capability may serve as a basis for defining the concept of an "ergodic" algorithm.
